The Law · Book 1 of 39

Genesis

"In the beginning was the Word" — and the Word is present in every beginning, every covenant, every story in this book. Genesis is not the story of how the world was made. It is the opening chapter of how the world was saved — and Jesus is on every page.

Genesis 1–2 · Creation — Jesus Was There

Genesis 1:1
"In the beginning, God created" — and the Word was already there
▼
The Big Idea

Jesus did not begin in Bethlehem. He was present and active at the very first moment of creation.

📖 What the Verse Says

"In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." Four words in Hebrew — Bereshit bara Elohim — and the entire story begins. But John 1:1–3 opens with an unmistakable echo: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... All things were made through him." John is not accidentally using Genesis language. He is telling every reader: go back to that very first moment — the Word was already there. Jesus was not a later addition to God's plan. He was the agent through whom everything that exists came into existence.

Paul confirms it in Colossians 1:16: "by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible." And again in Hebrews 1:2: God "has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world." The Son created the world He would one day enter to redeem it. The architect came to save the building He made.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • The Hebrew word Elohim is plural — "God" in Genesis 1 is a plural noun used with a singular verb. This grammatical tension in the very first verse hints at the multi-personal nature of God — Father, Son, and Spirit working as one. The Trinity is embedded in the grammar of Genesis 1:1.
  • "Created" (bara) is a word only used of God's action — never of human making. Jesus creates. He does not rearrange existing material. He speaks worlds into existence. This same creative authority appears in His miracles: He speaks and storms stop, bread multiplies, the dead rise.
  • Hebrews 11:3 — "By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God." The universe was spoken into existence. Jesus is the Word (John 1:1). The universe was created by Jesus.
New Testament Connection

John 1:1–3 — the Word was with God and was God at creation. Colossians 1:15–17 — Jesus is "the firstborn of all creation" and "all things were created through him and for him." Hebrews 1:2 — God created the world through His Son. Revelation 3:14 — Jesus is "the beginning of God's creation."

For Little Ones

"Before there were stars, before there were animals, before there was anything at all — Jesus was already there. He didn't just watch God make the world. He helped make it! Everything you can see — the trees, the sky, the animals, your hands — Jesus made it all. He is not just our Savior. He is our Creator."

For Teens

Colossians 1:17 says "in him all things hold together." This is not poetry — it is a cosmological statement. The universe does not sustain itself. It is sustained, moment by moment, by the ongoing will and power of Jesus. If He stopped sustaining it, it would cease to exist. Scientists study the forces that hold atoms together, that maintain the constants of physics — and the Bible says the answer behind all of those forces is a Person. How does it change your view of science, of nature, of daily life to know that Jesus is the reason everything keeps existing?

Family Discussion
  1. If Jesus made everything, what does that tell us about how He feels about creation? About us?
  2. John copied the words "In the beginning" from Genesis on purpose. What was he trying to tell us about Jesus?
  3. If Jesus is holding everything together right now, what does that mean for how we should treat the world He made?
Memory Verse
"All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made."
John 1:3
Genesis 1:2
The Spirit Hovering — The Pattern of New Creation
▼
The Big Idea

The Holy Spirit hovering over dark chaos before creation is the pattern God repeats every time He makes something new — including when He makes a person new.

📖 What the Verse Says

"The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters." Before a single word of creation is spoken, all three Persons of the Trinity are present: God the Father will speak, God the Son is the Word through whom He speaks, and God the Spirit is hovering — brooding, ready, poised over the dark formlessness like a mother bird over her nest. The Hebrew word rachaph for "hovering" is used in Deuteronomy 32:11 of an eagle hovering over its young to protect and carry them. The Spirit is tender, attentive, ready to bring forth life.

Then God speaks — and everything changes. Chaos becomes cosmos. Darkness becomes light. Emptiness becomes fullness. This is the pattern of all of God's creating and re-creating work.

🔍 How This Pattern Repeats Toward Jesus

  • At the conception of Jesus — Gabriel told Mary: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35). The same Spirit who hovered over the primordial waters overshadowed Mary, and the eternal Word took on flesh. A new creation — the incarnation — began the same way the first creation began: the Spirit hovering, God speaking.
  • At the baptism of Jesus — He came up from the water and "the Spirit of God descended like a dove and came to rest on him" (Matt. 3:16). The Spirit descended over the water again — announcing the new creation, the new Adam, the beginning of the new humanity.
  • At Pentecost — the disciples were gathered in formless fear, waiting. The Spirit came. The Church — the new creation community — was born. Genesis 1:2 repeated again.
  • At every conversion — Jesus told Nicodemus: "Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5). When the Spirit comes to a human soul, Genesis 1:2 happens in miniature: formless, dark, void — Spirit hovers — God speaks — new life begins. Every new birth in Christ is a new Genesis.
New Testament Connection

Luke 1:35 — the Spirit overshadowing Mary mirrors Gen 1:2. Matthew 3:16 — the Spirit descending at Jesus's baptism. John 3:5–8 — born of water and Spirit. 2 Corinthians 5:17 — "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." Acts 2:1–4 — Pentecost as a new creation event.

For Little Ones

"Before God made anything — before stars, animals, people, anything — the Spirit of God was hovering over the dark water. Like a bird hovering over a nest, getting ready. Then God SPOKE — and everything exploded into life. When Jesus rose from the dead, He breathed on His disciples and said 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' Same Spirit who made everything at the beginning — now living INSIDE the people who follow Jesus. The Creator lives in you."

Family Discussion
  1. The Spirit hovered over chaos before God created. Have you ever felt like your life was in chaos? What does this tell you about what God might be doing in those moments?
  2. The same Spirit that created the world lives in every Christian. What does that mean about the kind of power that is available to us?
  3. Every conversion is a "new creation." What things in your life look different because of the new creation — what "old" things have passed away?
Memory Verse
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come."
2 Corinthians 5:17
Genesis 1:3–5
Light Before the Sun — Jesus Is the True Light
▼
The Big Idea

Light existed for three days before the sun was created — because the true Light of the world is not a star. It is a Person.

📖 What the Verse Says

Day One: "And God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light. And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness." But the sun, moon, and stars are not created until Day Four (vv.14–19). Three days of light with no physical source. Where is it coming from? The text does not say. It simply says God spoke, and light appeared. This is not a scientific error or a pre-scientific cosmology — it is a deliberate theological statement: light does not depend on the sun. There is a light that precedes, transcends, and will outlast all physical luminaries.

🔍 Jesus Is That Light

John 1:4–5, 9: "In him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it... The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world." Jesus is not a lamp or a reflector. He is the source. He is the light itself.

Jesus said "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12; 9:5). Not "I have the light." Not "I know where the light is." He is the light — the same uncreated light that appeared on Day One before any star existed.

And look at how the Bible ends: Revelation 21:23 — "the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb." Revelation 22:5 — "night will be no more. They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light." The Bible begins with light before the sun and ends with light without the sun — and both times, that light is Jesus. The sun was always a temporary placeholder.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • "God saw that the light was good" — the Father looks at the light and declares it good. At Jesus's baptism, the Father speaks from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." The Father's delight in the light is the Father's delight in the Son.
  • Three days of light before the sun — three days without the expected source of light. Jesus was in the tomb three days — the light of the world hidden in darkness. And on the third day, He rose — the light returned, unextinguishable.
  • God separated light from darkness — Jesus said He came to bring division (Luke 12:51) — not physical war, but the cosmic separation of light from dark. Everyone who encounters Jesus must choose: remain in darkness or walk in the light.
  • 2 Corinthians 4:6 — "God, who said 'Let light shine out of darkness,' has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." Paul directly connects Genesis 1:3 to the moment of conversion — when God speaks light into a dark soul, it is the same creative act as Day One of creation.
New Testament Connection

John 1:4–9 — Jesus as the true light. John 8:12 — "I am the light of the world." 2 Corinthians 4:6 — God's creative word of light connected to the gospel shining in hearts. 1 John 1:5 — "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." Revelation 21:23; 22:5 — the new creation lit by the Lamb alone.

For Little Ones

Turn off all the lights in a room. Sit in the dark for a moment. Then turn on one light. Ask: "Where did the light come from? The light switch? The bulb? The electricity?" Keep tracing it back — power plant, fuel, the sun... Then say: "But what about before the sun existed? Where did God get light on Day One?" Let them think. "It came from God — from Jesus, who is the light of the world. The sun is just a light God made. Jesus is the real light that always was and always will be."

Family Discussion
  1. Why do you think God made light before He made the sun? What is He showing us?
  2. Jesus said "I am the light of the world." What does light do — practically? Name five things. Now connect each one to what Jesus does for His people.
  3. In the new creation (Revelation), there is no sun because Jesus is the light. What do you think that will be like? Does that sound better or worse than sunlight?
Memory Verse
"I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life."
John 8:12
Genesis 1:26–27
"Let Us Make Man" — The Image and the Image-Restorer
▼
The Big Idea

God made humans in His image — and when we broke that image through sin, Jesus came as the perfect Image of God to restore it in us.

📖 What the Verse Says

"Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.'" Two things demand attention immediately. First: "Let us" — God is speaking in the plural, within Himself. This is not God talking to angels (angels did not participate in creating humans). This is the eternal conversation within the Trinity — Father, Son, and Spirit consulting together to create humanity. Second: made "in our image" — the Hebrew word is tselem, the same word used for a statue or representation of a king. Humans were designed to be God's representatives on earth — walking portraits of the divine King, ruling on His behalf.

🔍 Jesus Is the Perfect Image — and He Restores Ours

Colossians 1:15 calls Jesus "the image of the invisible God." The Greek word is eikon — the exact image, the perfect representation. Adam was made in the image of God but distorted it through sin. Jesus IS the image of God — perfectly, permanently, undistorted. He is what Adam was supposed to be.

And He came to restore the image in us. 2 Corinthians 3:18: "we all... are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another." Romans 8:29: "those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son." The whole plan of salvation is God restoring the image He placed in us at creation — conforming us to look like Jesus, who is the perfect Image. Genesis 1:26–27 is the target; Romans 8:29 is the plan to restore it; and Jesus is both the restoration and the restorer.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • "Let us" — the plural is the first hint that God is not a solitary being. The Father, Son, and Spirit collaborate at the creation of humanity — and they collaborate equally at the redemption of humanity (the Father plans, the Son dies, the Spirit applies).
  • Made to have dominion (1:28) — God gave Adam dominion over all creation. Adam failed at that stewardship. Jesus, the Last Adam, exercises perfect dominion — "all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (Matt. 28:18). What Adam was given and lost, Jesus holds perfectly and permanently.
  • Male and female, both in God's image (1:27) — both men and women equally bear God's image. The dignity of every human person is grounded here. Jesus's ministry reflected this — He treated women with radical dignity in a culture that did not.
New Testament Connection

Colossians 1:15 — Jesus is "the image of the invisible God." Hebrews 1:3 — Jesus is "the exact imprint of his nature." Romans 8:29 — we are predestined to be conformed to Christ's image. 2 Corinthians 3:18 — we are being transformed into Christ's image. 1 Corinthians 15:45–49 — Jesus as the Last Adam who restores what the first Adam lost.

For Little Ones

Take a family photo. Point to your child and say: "You look like our family — you have some of Mom's eyes and Dad's nose. You bear the image of our family." Then say: "God made people to bear HIS image — to look like God in the way we love, think, and care for things. But sin broke that image — like a cracked mirror. Jesus came as the perfect Image of God — the uncracked mirror. And when we follow Jesus, He slowly fixes the mirror in us so we look more and more like God again."

Family Discussion
  1. What does it mean to bear God's image? Name three ways humans are different from animals that reflect being made in God's image.
  2. Sin "cracked" the image of God in humanity. What kinds of broken things do you see in people — including yourself — that are a result of that cracking?
  3. If Jesus is the perfect Image of God, and we are being conformed to His image — what does a person look like who is becoming more like Jesus? What specific qualities would you see?
Memory Verse
"He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation."
Colossians 1:15
Genesis 2:7
The Breath of Life — and the Breath of the Spirit
▼
The Big Idea

God breathed life into Adam's body — and after the resurrection, Jesus breathed the Holy Spirit into His disciples. The same breath that started humanity started the new humanity.

📖 What the Verse Says

"Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature." This is intimate and personal. God did not speak Adam into existence from a distance like He spoke the stars into being. He formed him — hands in the clay — and then bent close and breathed into him. The same Hebrew word for "breath" (neshamah) appears in Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones valley, where God breathes life into dead bones (Ezek. 37:9–10). God is the giver of breath — of physical life and spiritual life.

🔍 Jesus Repeats This Breath

John 20:22 — on the evening of the resurrection, Jesus appeared to the disciples and "breathed on them and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.'" The Greek word for "breathed on" (emphysao) is the same word used in the Septuagint (Greek OT) for Genesis 2:7 — "breathed into his nostrils." This is not accidental. John is making a direct connection: the same breath that gave physical life to Adam is now being given by the risen Jesus to bring spiritual life to His disciples — the birth of the new humanity.

The first Adam received the breath of God and became a living creature. The followers of the Last Adam receive the breath of the resurrected Christ and become a new creation. Genesis 2:7 is the type; John 20:22 is the fulfillment.

New Testament Connection

John 20:22 — Jesus breathes the Spirit on the disciples, directly echoing Gen 2:7. Ezekiel 37:9–10 — dry bones given breath — a resurrection preview. 1 Corinthians 15:45 — "The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit." Adam received breath; Jesus gives it.

For Little Ones

"God formed Adam out of dust — which is amazing enough. But then He did something more amazing: He leaned down and BREATHED into Adam's nostrils, and Adam came alive. God's own breath started the first human life! And after Jesus rose from the dead, He walked into a room where His scared disciples were hiding, and He breathed on them and said: 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' The same breath that started life in the first human started new life in the first Christians. That breath is still going — every person who follows Jesus receives that same Spirit."

Family Discussion
  1. God formed Adam from dust and breathed into him personally. What does this level of personal attention tell us about how God views each human being?
  2. Jesus breathed on His disciples the same way God breathed on Adam. What is He saying about the new creation He is starting?
  3. The Holy Spirit is sometimes called "the breath of God." In what ways does the Spirit give us life — not just at conversion, but day to day?
Memory Verse
"The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit."
1 Corinthians 15:45
Genesis 2:17
"You Shall Surely Die" — The Death Jesus Died Instead
▼
The Big Idea

God's warning in the Garden was real — disobedience brings death. Jesus took that death so we would not have to.

📖 What the Verse Says

"But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." The Hebrew is emphatic: mot tamut — "dying you shall die." This is not a mild warning. It is the foundational law of the moral universe — sin produces death. Not eventually, not maybe — but certainly. This is the law that drove everything that followed: every sacrifice, every priest, every death in the Old Testament is the echo of Genesis 2:17.

🔍 Jesus and the Death of Genesis 2:17

Romans 5:12 — "sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men." The "dying you shall die" of Genesis 2:17 is the death that came to all of Adam's descendants. Every human death is the consequence of that original warning being violated.

But Romans 5:17 continues: "if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ." The death of Genesis 2:17 — which every human inherits from Adam — was absorbed by Jesus at the cross. He died the death. He met the penalty. "Dying, He died" — so that we might live.

Hebrews 2:9 — "by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone." Jesus tasted the full cup of Genesis 2:17's penalty — so that everyone who is in Him is no longer subject to its verdict.

New Testament Connection

Romans 5:12–21 — the full Adam-Christ parallel, with death entering through Adam and life through Christ. Hebrews 2:9 — Jesus tasted death for everyone. 1 Corinthians 15:21–22 — "as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." Romans 6:23 — "the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord."

For Little Ones

"God gave Adam and Eve one rule. Just one! And He told them exactly what would happen if they broke it — 'you will die.' When they broke it, that's exactly what started happening. But here's the amazing part — Jesus came and took that punishment instead of us. The death that was supposed to come to us, He took. That's why the cross is the most important thing that ever happened."

Family Discussion
  1. God's warning was clear and serious. Why do you think Adam and Eve disobeyed anyway? Do we ever do the same thing — ignore clear warnings?
  2. "Dying you shall die" — what kinds of death do we experience as a result of sin? (Physical death, spiritual separation, broken relationships, inner emptiness...)
  3. Jesus "tasted death for everyone." What does it mean to you personally that Jesus drank the cup of Genesis 2:17 — so you don't have to?
Memory Verse
"For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord."
Romans 6:23
Genesis 2:18–25
The First Marriage — A Picture of Christ and the Church
▼
The Big Idea

Marriage was not invented by culture. It was designed by God to be a living portrait of Jesus's love for His Church — and that portrait was set up in Genesis 2 before sin ever entered the world.

📖 What the Verse Says

God says "It is not good that the man should be alone." He puts Adam into a deep sleep, takes a rib from his side, and forms the woman. Adam wakes and sees her for the first time: "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." God brings the woman to the man. They are "naked and were not ashamed." This is the first marriage — and God performed it. He was the first officiant.

🔍 Jesus, the Church, and the Mystery of Marriage

Ephesians 5:31–32 quotes Genesis 2:24 directly and then drops a stunning statement: "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church." Paul says the first marriage in Genesis 2 was always pointing forward to something bigger. The husband-wife relationship was designed as a living parable of Jesus and His people.

The parallels are precise: Adam was put into a deep sleep (a picture of death). From his side, a rib was taken (from Jesus's pierced side, water and blood flowed — John 19:34). From that wound, the Bride was formed. Adam woke to receive his bride. Jesus rose from the dead — and received His Bride, the Church. "Bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh" — Ephesians 5:30 says "we are members of his body." The Church is formed from the side of the dying and rising Christ, just as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • Adam's deep sleep — tardemah in Hebrew — is the same word used in Genesis 15:12 when God puts Abraham into a deep sleep before making the blood covenant. Deep sleep precedes God's most significant acts. Jesus's death is the "deep sleep" from which the Bride is formed.
  • The rib from Adam's side / the spear in Jesus's side — John 19:34 specifically mentions the soldier piercing Jesus's side, from which blood and water flowed. Blood and water are the elements of covenant and cleansing — the Bride of Christ is formed from His wounded side.
  • "Not ashamed" (2:25) — they were naked and unashamed. This is the state of perfection — total vulnerability, total safety, no shame. This is what Jesus restores: Revelation 19:8 says the Bride of Christ is clothed in white — she stands before God in total purity, no shame. What Genesis 2 had and Genesis 3 lost, Jesus restores in the end.
  • God brought the woman to the man — God is the matchmaker. He brings the Bride to the Son. Revelation 21:2 — "the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband." God presents the Bride.
New Testament Connection

Ephesians 5:25–32 — marriage points to Christ and the Church; Paul quotes Genesis 2:24. John 19:34 — water and blood from Jesus's side, echoing the rib from Adam's side. Revelation 19:7–9 — the Marriage Supper of the Lamb. Revelation 21:2 — the new Jerusalem as a bride.

For Little Ones

"God made the very first wedding! He made Eve from Adam's side — and then He brought her to Adam as a gift. Adam was so happy! God planned marriage to show us something about Jesus — Jesus loves His people (called His 'bride' in the Bible) the way the best husband loves the best wife. He gave everything for her. He will always be with her. And one day there will be the greatest wedding ever — when Jesus comes back for all His people."

Family Discussion
  1. Paul says marriage is a "mystery" that points to Christ and the Church. What things about a good marriage remind you of how Jesus loves His people?
  2. Eve was formed from Adam's side while he slept. The Church was formed from Jesus's pierced side while He died. What does that tell you about the cost of the Bride to Jesus?
  3. Adam and Eve were "naked and not ashamed." What does it mean to stand before God with no shame? Is that possible for us? How?
Memory Verse
"This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church."
Ephesians 5:32

Genesis 3 · The Fall — And the First Promise of a Savior

Genesis 3:1–7
The Serpent, the Lie, and the Broken Image
▼
The Big Idea

The serpent's strategy — "Did God really say?" — is the oldest lie in existence. Jesus defeated it not by arguing but by trusting.

📖 What the Verse Says

The serpent comes to Eve with a question designed to create doubt: "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?" This is a slight distortion — God had said they could eat from every tree except one. The serpent misquotes God, making the restriction seem much larger than it is. Eve corrects the quote — but she also slightly misquotes God, adding "neither shall you touch it" (God hadn't said that). She is already being drawn off-center. Then the serpent attacks directly: "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God." Three lies in one: God's word cannot be trusted; God is withholding something good from you; you can become your own god. She eats. She gives to Adam who eats. Their eyes are opened — and what they see is their own nakedness. They made fig leaves. They hid.

🔍 Jesus and the Three Temptations

Luke 4:1–13 — Jesus is led into the wilderness and tempted by the devil for forty days. The temptations parallel Genesis 3 exactly. Satan attacks the same three points: Doubt God's provision — "If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread." Adam took what God had not provided; Jesus refused to act outside the Father's will. Doubt God's protection — "throw yourself down, and angels will catch you." Satan even quotes Scripture. Jesus answers with Scripture. The offer of godhood apart from God — "All these kingdoms I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." Adam and Eve grasped at being "like God" through disobedience; Jesus refused to grasp at glory except through the Father's path. Where Adam failed all three, Jesus defeated all three — with nothing but Scripture and trust. Jesus succeeded in the wilderness where Adam and Israel both failed.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • "Did God actually say?" — Satan's primary weapon is always a question mark placed after God's word. Jesus answers every temptation with "It is written." The Word of God is the weapon against the distortion of God's word.
  • Adam was present (3:6) — "she also gave some to her husband who was with her." Adam was not off somewhere else. He was right there and said nothing. He failed to lead, protect, or stand in the gap. Jesus, the Last Adam, does the opposite — He stands in the gap, steps forward, and takes the blow.
  • They hid among the trees (3:8) — they used creation to hide from the Creator. Jesus was crucified outside the city, in the open — He did not hide. He came into the full light of judgment willingly.
  • Revelation 12:9 calls the dragon "that ancient serpent." The enemy in Genesis 3 and the enemy in Revelation are the same being — and he is defeated by "the blood of the Lamb" (Rev. 12:11).
New Testament Connection

Luke 4:1–13 — Jesus's temptation as the reversal of Genesis 3. Romans 5:19 — "by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners; by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous." Revelation 12:9, 11 — the ancient serpent defeated by the blood of the Lamb.

For Little Ones

"The serpent told Eve: 'Did God really say that?' He was trying to make her doubt God's words. And it worked — she ate the fruit. But when the devil tried the same trick on Jesus — 'Did God really say you have to do things His way?' — Jesus said 'It is written!' and used God's word like a sword to fight back. Jesus won the fight that Adam lost. And because Jesus won, we can win too."

Family Discussion
  1. The serpent's first move was to question God's word. How does that same strategy work in our lives today? What are modern versions of "Did God really say...?"
  2. Adam was right there when Eve was being deceived and said nothing. Where does that failure show up in your own life — times when you stayed silent when you should have spoken?
  3. Jesus defeated every temptation by quoting Scripture. What does that tell you about how important it is to know the Bible? What happens when we don't know what "it is written"?
Memory Verse
"For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous."
Romans 5:19
Genesis 3:8–13
"Where Are You?" — The God Who Comes Looking
▼
The Big Idea

The first thing God did after the fall was come looking for the ones who hid from Him. That seeking nature of God is fully revealed in Jesus.

📖 What the Verse Says

"And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, 'Where are you?'" God knows exactly where Adam is. This is not a search query. It is a call — an invitation to come out of hiding. God's first response to the fall is not a lightning bolt. It is a walk in the garden and a voice calling out a name. He comes. He seeks. He asks.

🔍 Jesus Is the "Where Are You?" Made Flesh

Luke 19:10 — Jesus said "The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost." This is the theological statement of His entire mission — and it is rooted in Genesis 3:8–9. The God who walked in the garden calling "where are you?" eventually walked among us in flesh, still seeking the hidden, still calling the lost by name.

Luke 15 — Jesus tells three parables about seeking: the shepherd who leaves 99 to find 1, the woman who searches her whole house for 1 coin, the father who runs to meet his returning son. All three are God's answer to Genesis 3:9 — "where are you?" I am coming to find you. The initiative is always His.

John 20:15–16 — Mary Magdalene is weeping at the empty tomb. She thinks Jesus is the gardener. He says one word: "Mary." She turns and recognizes Him. The risen Jesus is walking in a garden, calling a name — the exact image of Genesis 3:8–9. Adam and Eve hid in the garden from the walking God who called. Mary was found in a garden by the walking God who called her name. What was lost in a garden is found in a garden.

New Testament Connection

Luke 19:10 — "The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost." Luke 15:3–32 — the three "seeking" parables. John 20:15–16 — Jesus in the garden, calling Mary's name. John 10:3 — "He calls his own sheep by name."

For Little Ones

"When Adam and Eve sinned, they hid from God — they were ashamed and scared. But God came walking in the garden and called out: 'Where are you?' He wasn't asking because He didn't know. He was giving them a chance to come out. God always comes looking for the ones who are hiding. Luke 19:10 says Jesus came 'to seek and to save the lost.' That's what the whole Bible is — God walking through the garden calling 'where are you?' and people slowly coming out of hiding."

Family Discussion
  1. Adam and Eve hid from God. Do we ever hide from God? What does "hiding from God" look like in real life?
  2. "Where are you?" — God asked this question knowing the answer. Why do you think He asked? What was He giving Adam the chance to do?
  3. Jesus in John 20 is in a garden, calling a name. Adam and Eve hid in a garden from God's voice. What does the contrast between those two scenes tell us about what Jesus accomplished?
Memory Verse
"For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost."
Luke 19:10
Genesis 3:15
The First Gospel — The Promise of Jesus in the Curse
▼
The Big Idea

In the darkest moment of human history — the very chapter where sin entered — God announced the gospel. Before any prayer was uttered, before any repentance expressed, the promise of Jesus was made.

📖 What the Verse Says

"I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." God is speaking to the serpent. Every word is loaded. This is called the Protoevangelium — the "first gospel" — and theologians have marveled at it for thousands of years. It is the seed of the entire Bible planted in the third chapter of the first book.

🔍 Every Word Points to Jesus

  • "The seed of the woman" — in all of Hebrew genealogy, "seed" always traces through the father. Women do not have seed; men do. This is the only time in the entire Old Testament where "seed of the woman" is used — and it points unmistakably to a child born without a human father. Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, born of woman." The virgin birth was announced in Genesis 3.
  • "He shall bruise your head" — a head wound is mortal. Crushing a head kills. This describes the final, decisive defeat of the serpent — which Jesus accomplished at the cross. Colossians 2:15: "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him." Hebrews 2:14: "through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil."
  • "You shall bruise his heel" — a heel wound hurts but does not kill. This is the cross — the serpent wounded Jesus through His betrayal, suffering, and death. It was a real wound. But it was not fatal to the divine purpose. Jesus rose. The heel healed. The head did not.
  • Grace precedes everything — God makes this promise before Adam and Eve express any repentance, before they pray, before they do anything. The gospel is announced unprompted. This is the pattern of grace — God initiates always.
  • This promise drives all of history — from Genesis 3:15 forward, the entire Old Testament is the story of God protecting and preparing the "seed of the woman" — the line through which the Savior would come. Every genealogy, every covenant, every king of David's line is a chapter in this story.
"I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."Genesis 3:15
New Testament Connection

Galatians 4:4 — "born of woman" fulfills "seed of the woman." Colossians 2:15 — the head-crushing at the cross. Hebrews 2:14 — Jesus destroys the one who has the power of death. Romans 16:20 — "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet." Revelation 12:9; 20:10 — the serpent's final defeat.

For Little Ones

"Genesis 3:15 is the very first promise in the Bible — and it's about Jesus. God told the serpent: 'I will put hatred between you and the woman, between your seed and her Seed. He will crush your head, and you will bruise his heel.' The serpent would wound the Seed — that's the cross. The Seed would crush the serpent's head — that's the resurrection. The bruise on the heel is temporary. The crushed head is permanent. Jesus won. From the very first book, the very first chapters, God was already announcing the victory."

Family Discussion
  1. God made the gospel promise before Adam and Eve even asked for help. What does that tell us about who initiates in our relationship with God — us or Him?
  2. "Seed of the woman" is the first hint of the virgin birth. How does it change your view of the Christmas story to know it was promised in Genesis 3?
  3. The serpent bruised Jesus's heel — real pain, real death. But Jesus crushed the serpent's head — a mortal wound. Why is it important that Jesus actually suffered, even though He ultimately won?
Memory Verse
"But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law."
Galatians 4:4–5
Genesis 3:21
Garments of Skin — The First Sacrifice for Sin
▼
The Big Idea

The first death in Scripture was God killing an animal to clothe the ashamed. From that moment to the cross, the entire Bible is about innocent blood covering sinful humanity.

📖 What the Verse Says

"And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them." Adam and Eve had made their own covering — fig leaves stitched together (3:7). It was the first act of religious self-effort. God replaced it. For skins to exist, an animal had to die. The Bible does not name the animal. It does not describe the killing. It simply states the result: God made garments. God clothed them. Something innocent died so their shame could be covered, and God was the one who provided and applied the covering.

🔍 The Whole Logic of the Gospel in One Verse

This single verse contains the entire theological structure of salvation: Sin → Shame → Human effort insufficient → Innocent death → God provides covering → God applies it personally. Every sacrifice from this moment to the cross follows this pattern. And the cross is where God provides the final, permanent covering — not animal skin, but the righteousness of His own Son.

The Hebrew word for atonement is kaphar — "to cover." Atonement is covering. Genesis 3:21 is the first act of atonement in Scripture. God covered their shame with the skin of a dead animal. The cross is God covering our shame with the blood of His Son. The pattern is identical; the scale is incomparably greater.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • Fig leaves failed — self-made religion never works. Every human attempt to cover sin with our own effort — morality, religious ritual, good works, self-improvement — is a fig leaf. God accepts none of it as covering. Only His provision covers.
  • God did the work — He did not leave the skins in a pile for them to pick up. "The LORD God... clothed them." He personally dressed them. This is not a transaction — it is an act of tender fatherly care. God clothed the ashamed the way a parent dresses a child.
  • Isaiah 61:10 — "He has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness." The "clothing" language of Genesis 3:21 grows into the robe of righteousness — and it is God who gives it, not our own weaving.
  • Romans 13:14; Galatians 3:27 — "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ." "You have clothed yourselves with Christ." Salvation is being clothed in Christ's righteousness — the ultimate fulfillment of God clothing the ashamed in Genesis 3:21.
New Testament Connection

2 Corinthians 5:21 — the great exchange: our sin for His righteousness. Romans 13:14 — "put on the Lord Jesus Christ." Galatians 3:27 — "clothed with Christ." Revelation 7:14 — robes washed in the blood of the Lamb. Revelation 19:8 — the Bride clothed in fine linen (the righteous deeds of the saints — given by Christ).

For Little Ones

"Adam and Eve tried to cover their shame themselves — they sewed fig leaves together. But fig leaves don't last. So God made proper clothes for them — from animal skins. Which means an animal had to die to cover them. That's the first sacrifice in the Bible — an animal dying so humans could be covered. That's the picture of everything Jesus would do: He died so we could be covered. Revelation 19:8 says the Bride of Christ is dressed in 'fine linen, bright and pure' — the righteousness of the saints. God is still in the business of replacing our fig leaves with something that actually covers."

Family Discussion
  1. What is the difference between Adam and Eve's fig leaves and God's garments of skin? What does that difference represent?
  2. Something had to die to cover their shame. Why do you think God required that? What does it teach us about the cost of sin?
  3. God clothed them — He did the work. What does it mean in practice that salvation is something God does to us, not something we do ourselves?
Memory Verse
"For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God."
2 Corinthians 5:21

Genesis 4 · Cain & Abel — Accepted and Rejected

Genesis 4:1–8
The Two Offerings — Blood Accepted, Works Rejected
▼
The Big Idea

From the very first act of worship in human history, God established: He accepts the blood sacrifice offered in faith, not the works-offering of self-effort.

📖 What the Verse Says

Cain brings "an offering of the fruit of the ground." Abel brings "the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions." God has regard for Abel's offering; He does not for Cain's. Cain's fury leads him to murder his brother. When God confronts him, Cain denies knowledge of Abel's fate with the famous question: "Am I my brother's keeper?" Then God declares: "Your brother's blood is crying out to me from the ground."

🔍 How This Points to Jesus

Why was Abel's offering accepted? Hebrews 11:4 answers: "By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice." It was faith — but what did the faith express? Abel brought blood — the life of the firstborn. He understood from Genesis 3:21 that approaching God required an innocent death. Cain brought what he made with his own hands. God was not impressed. He never is by self-effort. This is not an arbitrary preference — it is the consistent theological statement of the whole Bible: human works cannot cover sin; only substitutionary blood can.

Abel is a type of Christ: He was righteous (Jesus called him "righteous Abel," Matt. 23:35). He was killed by his own family — hated and murdered for his righteousness, just as Jesus was rejected and crucified by His own people. His blood cried from the ground for justice. Jesus's blood, shed unjustly at the same hands, cries for something far greater.

Hebrews 12:24 — "Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel." Abel's blood cried: avenge me, punish the murderer. Jesus's blood cries: forgive them, spare the guilty. The same kind of innocent blood, shed unjustly — but utterly different cries. Abel's blood demanded justice. Jesus's blood purchases mercy.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • "Sin is crouching at the door" (4:7) — first use of the word "sin" in the Bible. God describes it as a predator waiting outside — not a mistake or a weakness but a power that hunts. Jesus came to "destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8) — the one who empowers this crouching predator.
  • "Am I my brother's keeper?" (4:9) — the unspoken answer is yes. And Jesus is the ultimate answer. He IS our Keeper. The Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11). Cain refused to keep his brother; Jesus keeps us at the cost of His own life.
  • Cain was driven from God's presence (4:16) — the wages of sin is exile from God. Jesus bore that exile — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matt. 27:46) — so that we would not have to be driven away.
  • God put a mark on Cain to protect him (4:15) — even in judgment, God preserved life. Even the murderer received mercy. This is the strange persistence of God's grace — it runs toward even the least deserving. Jesus died for Cain-like people — for the very ones who crucified Him.
New Testament Connection

Hebrews 11:4 — Abel's offering by faith. Hebrews 12:24 — Jesus's blood speaks better than Abel's. Matthew 23:35 — Jesus calls Abel "righteous." 1 John 3:12 — Cain killed Abel because Abel's deeds were righteous — same motive as the crucifixion. John 10:11 — Jesus as the Keeper who lays down His life.

For Little Ones

"Cain brought vegetables. Abel brought a lamb. God was happy with Abel's offering — the one with blood — and not with Cain's. Why? Because from the very beginning, God was teaching His people that sins require a sacrifice — something has to die in our place. Abel understood that. Cain didn't. And that's what Jesus is — the final Lamb, who died in our place so God can accept us." Then: "Abel's blood cried out from the ground. But Jesus's blood is louder — and it cries 'forgive them!'

Family Discussion
  1. Both brothers brought offerings — but only one was accepted. The content AND the heart mattered. What does it mean to come to God "in faith"? What makes religious activity genuine vs. empty?
  2. Cain murdered his brother because Abel was righteous and he wasn't. The religious leaders crucified Jesus for the same reason. What does this tell us about how unrighteousness responds to righteousness?
  3. Abel's blood cried for vengeance. Jesus's blood cries for forgiveness. Which cry is harder to utter? What does it tell you about the character of Jesus that His blood cries for mercy?
Memory Verse
"...and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel."
Hebrews 12:24

Genesis 5 · The Genealogy of Life — and a Hidden Message

Genesis 5:1–32
The Names That Preach the Gospel
▼
The Big Idea

Even in a list of names — the part of the Bible most people skip — God embedded the message of the gospel and the promise of Jesus.

📖 What the Verse Says

Genesis 5 lists ten generations from Adam to Noah, noting for each: who they fathered, how long they lived, and that "he died." The phrase "and he died" rings like a funeral bell through the chapter — an echo of the warning in Genesis 2:17. But the chapter also contains the genealogical line through which Noah — and ultimately Jesus — would come. And there is something hidden in the Hebrew meanings of these ten names that has astonished Bible scholars.

🔍 The Hidden Gospel in the Names

When you translate the ten names of Genesis 5 from Hebrew into English, they form a sentence: Adam (Man) — Seth (Appointed) — Enosh (Mortal) — Kenan (Sorrow) — Mahalalel (The Blessed God) — Jared (Shall come down) — Enoch (Teaching) — Methuselah (His death shall bring) — Lamech (Despairing) — Noah (Rest, comfort).

Reading them together: "Man appointed mortal sorrow. The Blessed God shall come down teaching. His death shall bring the despairing rest." This is the gospel in ten names — hidden in a genealogy that most readers skip. God embedded the story of Jesus in the very names of Adam's descendants, written into the fabric of Genesis before Moses composed a single line of Exodus.

🔍 Enoch — Taken Without Dying

In a chapter where "and he died" appears seven times, one man breaks the pattern: "Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him" (5:24). Enoch did not die. He was taken. Hebrews 11:5 says "by faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him." Enoch is a type of the resurrection and rapture — the first picture in Scripture of someone going to be with God without passing through death. Jesus is the Resurrection and the Life (John 11:25). Because of Him, those who are alive at His return "will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thess. 4:17) — the ultimate fulfillment of what happened to Enoch.

🔍 Methuselah — The Longest Life and a Hidden Warning

Methuselah lived 969 years — the longest human life in Scripture. His name means "his death shall bring" or "when he is dead it shall be sent." Jewish tradition holds that the flood came the same year Methuselah died. If true, his very name was a 969-year countdown to judgment — and God, in His mercy, delayed the flood as long as Methuselah lived. The patience of God is written into the lifespan of one man. 2 Peter 3:9: "The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance." Methuselah's long life is a picture of God's patience before judgment — a patience that reaches its ultimate expression in the long years before Jesus returns.

New Testament Connection

Hebrews 11:5 — Enoch's translation without death. 1 Thessalonians 4:17 — the living caught up at Christ's return, like Enoch. Jude 14 — Enoch prophesied Christ's second coming. 2 Peter 3:9 — God's patience before judgment, like Methuselah's long life. Luke 3:23–38 — Jesus's genealogy traces back through these same names to Adam.

For Little Ones

"This chapter keeps saying 'and he died, and he died, and he died.' But then there is one man — Enoch — who didn't die! God just took him. Why? Because he walked with God every day. Enoch shows us what life with Jesus will be like — one day, Jesus will come back and take us to be with Him. We don't have to be afraid of death if we are walking with God."

Family Discussion
  1. If the names of Genesis 5 spell out the gospel, what does that tell us about how carefully God planned the story of salvation — even in the parts of the Bible that seem boring?
  2. Enoch "walked with God" for 365 years. What do you think that looked like day to day? What would "walking with God" look like for you this week?
  3. Methuselah's long life was God's patience before judgment. In what ways do you see God's patience — toward the world, and toward you personally?
Memory Verse
"By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him."
Hebrews 11:5

Genesis 6–9 · Noah & the Ark — Salvation Through Judgment

Genesis 6:1–22
The Ark — Every Detail Points to Jesus
▼
The Big Idea

The ark was not just a boat. It was a detailed, three-dimensional picture of salvation in Jesus Christ — with one door, a blood-covering, God shutting the door, and new life emerging from judgment.

📖 What the Verse Says

Humanity has become so corrupt that "every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (6:5) and God "was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart" (6:6). But "Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD" (6:8) — the first use of the word "grace" in Scripture. God gives Noah detailed instructions to build an ark. Noah "did all that God commanded him" (6:22). The construction of the ark is obedient faith responding to a warning about things not yet seen — Hebrews 11:7's definition of faith perfectly described.

🔍 Detail-by-Detail Typology of the Ark

  • One door (6:16) — God specified one door. Not multiple entrances — one. Jesus said: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). "There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). The ark's one door is the first architectural statement of the exclusivity of salvation through Christ alone.
  • Pitch inside and out — kaphar (6:14) — God told Noah to cover the ark inside and out with pitch. The Hebrew word is kaphar — the exact root of the word "atonement" throughout Leviticus. The ark was literally "atoned" — covered with a substance that would keep out the waters of judgment. The atonement of the cross keeps out the judgment of God from all who are inside Christ. The ark floated in the middle of God's wrath — totally covered, totally secure.
  • God shut the door (7:16) — "and the LORD shut him in." Noah did not shut the door. God did. The one who provides salvation is the one who seals it. Ephesians 1:13: "In him you also... were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit." God seals His people inside. No one can open what God has shut (Rev. 3:7).
  • Eight souls saved (7:13) — the number eight in Scripture consistently signals new beginning and resurrection (Jesus rose on the eighth day — the first day of the new week). Eight people passed through the waters of judgment and emerged into a new world. This is baptism arithmetic — death and resurrection.
  • The same water destroyed and saved — the flood killed those outside the ark; the same water carried the ark to safety. 1 Peter 3:20–21 makes this explicit: the flood "corresponds" to baptism. You pass through the water of judgment; if you are in Christ, it carries you to new life rather than drowning you.
  • Noah found grace before he did anything righteous (6:8–9) — verse 8 says he found grace; verse 9 says he was righteous. Grace came first. Righteousness was the result, not the cause. This is the gospel order: God's grace precedes our obedience.
New Testament Connection

1 Peter 3:20–21 — the flood and the ark correspond to baptism — saved through water. John 10:9 — "I am the door." Acts 4:12 — no other name. Hebrews 11:7 — Noah's faith. Matthew 24:37–39 — Jesus uses Noah's day as a picture of the days before His return. Ephesians 1:13 — sealed by the Spirit, like God shutting the door.

For Little Ones

Build a simple "ark" from a box. Put toy animals and people inside. Then "close the door" yourself. Say: "When Noah and his family were inside, God shut the door — not Noah. God sealed them safe inside. That's what Jesus does for us — when we trust in Him, God seals us safe inside His love. The storm raged outside — but inside the ark, with God, they were safe."

Family Discussion
  1. The ark had one door — and God shut it. How does the "one door" of the ark help us understand what Jesus means when He says "I am the door"? What happens to those who are outside?
  2. The word for pitch — kaphar — is the same root as atonement. What does it mean that the ark was "atoned"? How does Jesus's atonement work the same way — covering us so judgment cannot reach us?
  3. Noah found grace before he was called righteous. How does the order (grace first, then righteousness) show up in the Christian life today?
Memory Verse
"...eight persons, were brought safely through water. Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you... through the resurrection of Jesus Christ."
1 Peter 3:20–21
Genesis 8:1–9:17
New World, New Covenant, the Dove and the Rainbow
▼
The Big Idea

After the judgment, God makes a covenant of peace — marked by a rainbow — and the symbols of new life (the dove, the olive branch, the altar) all point to the gospel.

📖 What the Verse Says

"But God remembered Noah." The waters recede. The ark rests on Ararat. Noah sends out a raven — it does not return. Then a dove — it returns with nothing. Then a dove again — it returns with an olive branch, the sign that life has returned to the earth. Noah opens the ark. God tells them to come out. Noah's first act is to build an altar and offer burnt offerings. God smells the pleasing aroma and says He will never again curse the ground or destroy all life with a flood. He establishes a covenant with Noah, his family, and every living creature. He sets a bow — a rainbow — in the clouds as the sign.

🔍 Jesus in the Details

  • "God remembered Noah" (8:1) — in Hebrew, "remember" is not merely calling something to mind. It is active engagement — God acting on behalf of someone. When God "remembers" someone in Scripture, deliverance follows (see also Gen. 30:22; Exod. 2:24). This is the first use of this covenant language — and it points to the ultimate "remembering" in Jesus. The thief on the cross said "remember me when you come into your kingdom" (Luke 23:42). Jesus answered immediately.
  • The raven vs. the dove — the raven went out and did not return — it found sustenance in the carnage, in the things of death. The dove could find no rest — no place to land — and returned to the ark. On its second flight it returned with an olive branch — the first sign of new life, of peace, of resurrection. The dove is universally associated with the Holy Spirit (Matt. 3:16) — the Spirit who rests only where there is life, peace, and the presence of God.
  • Noah's first act was worship (8:20) — he built an altar and sacrificed burnt offerings. The first act of the new humanity emerging from judgment is worship. This is the pattern for the redeemed: rescued → worship. And Revelation 5:9–14 shows the redeemed in the new creation doing exactly this — worshipping the Lamb who saved them.
  • The rainbow covenant (9:12–17) — a bow is a weapon. God hung His weapon in the sky — pointed upward, away from the earth, toward heaven. It is an act of divine self-binding: I will take the arrow of my own judgment rather than turn it on you. At the cross, that is exactly what happened. God directed His own wrath toward His own Son rather than toward His people. Revelation 4:3 — there is a rainbow around the throne of God in heaven. The covenant mercy of the rainbow is permanently memorialized before the throne.
New Testament Connection

Luke 23:42–43 — "remember me" / "today you will be with me in paradise." Matthew 3:16 — the dove at Jesus's baptism. Revelation 4:3 — the rainbow around God's throne. Revelation 5:9–14 — the redeemed worshipping the Lamb. Isaiah 54:9–10 — God references the Noahic covenant as a picture of His unbreakable love in the new covenant.

For Little Ones

"After the flood, the very first thing Noah did when he got off the boat was build an altar and say 'thank you' to God. Not 'where do I live now?' or 'what's for dinner?' — the FIRST thing was worship. When we have been rescued by Jesus from something really scary, what should our first response be? And see the rainbow? Every time you see a rainbow, God is reminding us: 'I keep my promises. I am faithful. I will not abandon you.'"

Family Discussion
  1. "God remembered Noah" — not just in thought but in action. Do you ever feel forgotten by God? What does His "remembering" of Noah tell you about how He thinks about you?
  2. A bow is a weapon — and God pointed it away from the earth, toward heaven. How does the cross show the same thing? Where did God's wrath go?
  3. Noah's first act after rescue was worship. What is usually your first response after God has helped you or rescued you from something? What would it look like to make worship the first response?
Memory Verse
"For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed, says the LORD, who has compassion on you."
Isaiah 54:10

Genesis 10–11 · The Nations and Babel — Scattered to Be Gathered

Genesis 11:1–9
The Tower of Babel — Reversed at Pentecost
▼
The Big Idea

Humanity united in pride to reach God on their own terms — God scattered them. At Pentecost, Jesus reunited humanity through the Spirit on God's terms.

📖 What the Verse Says

All humanity shares one language and settles in Shinar. They say: "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves." God comes down, sees it, and confuses their language — scattering them across the earth. The project collapses. The city is called Babel — from the word for "confusion." The pride of humanity trying to ascend to God results in division, confusion, and scattering.

🔍 Jesus and the Reversal of Babel

Acts 2:1–11 — Pentecost is the direct reversal of Babel. At Babel: one language → confusion → many languages → scattering → disunity. At Pentecost: many languages → the Spirit → one message understood by all → gathering → unity. People from every nation under heaven heard the gospel in their own language (Acts 2:8–11) — the languages that were divided at Babel were simultaneously transcended at Pentecost by the power of the Holy Spirit.

Babel asked: "How do we ascend to God?" The answer was: you can't. God must descend to you. And that is exactly what He did — first in the incarnation (the Word became flesh, John 1:14), then in the Spirit (the Spirit came down at Pentecost, Acts 2:2–4). God always descends to humanity. Humanity cannot ascend to God except through the One who came down first.

Revelation 7:9–10 — the ultimate reversal of Babel: "a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb." What Babel divided, the Lamb reunites. The nations scattered at Babel are gathered around the throne of Jesus in Revelation — every language, every people, united in worship. The scattering is reversed; the gathering is complete.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • "Let us make a name for ourselves" (11:4) — this is the sin behind the sin. The desire to be remembered, to be great, to be famous — independent of God. Jesus emptied Himself of reputation (Phil. 2:7) — He made Himself of no name. And God exalted Him above every name (Phil. 2:9). You lose the name you grasp; you receive the name you surrender.
  • "Let us go down" (11:7) — God uses the plural again: "Let us go down and there confuse their language." The Trinity descends together to deal with human pride — just as the Trinity would later descend together in the incarnation and at Pentecost.
  • The Great Commission (Matt. 28:19–20) — "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations." Jesus sends His people back to the nations that were scattered at Babel — to gather them with the gospel, in anticipation of the great reunion before the throne.
New Testament Connection

Acts 2:1–11 — Pentecost as the reversal of Babel. Philippians 2:7–9 — Jesus emptied Himself of name; God gave Him THE name. Matthew 28:19 — go to all nations Babel scattered. Revelation 7:9–10 — all nations gathered around the Lamb. John 1:14 — the Word descended — the answer to Babel's question.

For Little Ones

"The people at Babel said 'Let's build a tower so we can get UP to God.' But God said 'No — that's not how it works.' So He scattered them. But then Jesus came — God came DOWN to us. We can't get to God by climbing up. He comes to us. And at Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came down and let people from every country hear about Jesus in their own language — the very countries that got scattered at Babel were all brought back together by the gospel."

Family Discussion
  1. The people at Babel wanted to "make a name for themselves." What are modern versions of that — ways people try to make their own name and reputation the center of their life?
  2. Babel divided people by language. The gospel of Jesus unites people across every language and culture. What does that unity look like in your church, your community?
  3. At Babel, humanity tried to ascend to God. At Pentecost, God descended to humanity. What does this pattern — God always comes to us — mean for how we approach our relationship with Him?
Memory Verse
"After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb."
Revelation 7:9

Genesis 12–13 · The Call of Abram — The Covenant That Becomes the Gospel

Genesis 12:1–3
"In You All the Families of the Earth Shall Be Blessed"
▼
The Big Idea

The promise God made to Abraham is the promise of Jesus — Paul says so explicitly. The "blessing" God promised to all nations through Abraham is the gospel of Christ.

📖 What the Verse Says

God calls Abram out of Ur with a staggering promise: "I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing... and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." Five "I will" statements — God binding Himself by promise to one man and, through him, to all the nations of the earth. This is the Abrahamic covenant — the backbone of the entire Old Testament and the seed of the New.

🔍 Paul's Interpretation: This IS the Gospel

Galatians 3:8 — "And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.'" Paul says the promise of Genesis 12:3 IS the gospel. God was not making vague promises about cultural influence. He was announcing that through Abraham's lineage, Jesus Christ would come — and through Jesus, every family on earth would have access to the blessing of right standing with God.

Galatians 3:16 goes further: "Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, 'And to offsprings,' referring to many, but referring to one, 'And to your offspring,' who is Christ." The singular "offspring" (Hebrew: zera) is Jesus. The promise to Abraham is a promise about Jesus. Everything in the covenant with Abraham — the land, the nation, the blessing to all nations — finds its ultimate fulfillment not in Israel as a political entity but in Jesus Christ and those who are in Him (Gal. 3:29: "if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise").

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • "Go from your country" (12:1) — Abram had to leave everything familiar and go to a place God would show him. Hebrews 11:8 — "By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going." Jesus left the glory of heaven — "the place he knew" — and came to a world that was alien to His holiness. The call to leave for an unknown destination is a picture of the incarnation.
  • "I will make your name great" — contrast with Babel — at Babel, humanity tried to make their own name great and failed. God promised to make Abram's name great — not because of Abram's effort but as a gift of grace. Jesus, who made Himself of no reputation, received the name above every name (Phil. 2:9). God makes great the name of those who do not grasp for greatness.
  • "All the families of the earth" — not just Israel. Not just the circumcised. All families. Romans 4:13: Abraham is "heir of the world" — the promise reaches every ethnicity, every culture, every language. The gospel is for all.
New Testament Connection

Galatians 3:8 — Genesis 12:3 is the gospel preached in advance. Galatians 3:16 — the "offspring" is Christ. Galatians 3:29 — we are Abraham's heirs through Christ. Romans 4:13 — Abraham heir of the world. Acts 3:25 — Peter quotes Genesis 12:3 and says it is fulfilled in Jesus. Revelation 7:9 — all nations blessed, gathered around the Lamb.

For Little Ones

"God made an amazing promise to a man named Abram — 'through you, every family in the entire world will be blessed.' Every family! That means your family, and families in China, and families in Africa, and families everywhere. How can one man's family bless the WHOLE world? Through Jesus — Jesus came from Abram's family. And Jesus is the blessing for the whole world."

Family Discussion
  1. Paul says the promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 IS the gospel preached in advance. How does knowing the gospel was announced in Genesis — before the Law, before Moses, before Israel — change how you think about the relationship between the Old and New Testaments?
  2. Abram left his home country with no map, no GPS, no specific destination — just God's word. What does that kind of faith look like in practical, modern life?
  3. The blessing was for "all families of the earth" — not just one nation. How does the universal scope of God's promise change how you think about mission, about reaching people from different cultures and backgrounds?
Memory Verse
"And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, 'In you shall all the nations be blessed.'"
Galatians 3:8

Genesis 14 · Melchizedek — The Eternal Priest-King

Genesis 14:18–20
Melchizedek — Bread, Wine, and the Pre-Incarnate Priest
▼
The Big Idea

Melchizedek appears with no beginning and no end, combines the offices of king and priest, brings bread and wine, and blesses Abraham — and the New Testament says he was a living portrait of Jesus's eternal priesthood.

📖 What the Verse Says

After Abraham's military victory, a mysterious figure appears: "Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.) And he blessed him and said, 'Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!' And Abram gave him a tenth of everything." Three verses. No genealogy. No origin story. No death recorded. He brings bread and wine. He blesses. He receives tithes. Then he is gone — until Psalm 110 and Hebrews devote enormous attention to unpacking who he was.

🔍 Every Detail Points to Jesus

  • King of Righteousness — "Melchizedek" in Hebrew means "king of righteousness." Jesus is our righteousness (1 Cor. 1:30) and the righteous King (Jer. 23:5–6).
  • King of Salem = King of Peace — "Salem" means "peace." Salem later becomes Jerusalem. Jesus is the Prince of Peace (Isa. 9:6) and "He himself is our peace" (Eph. 2:14).
  • Priest AND King simultaneously — Israel\'s law strictly separated these offices. Only Levites could be priests; only Davidic descendants could be kings. Uzziah was struck with leprosy for trying to combine them (2 Chr. 26:16–21). But Melchizedek holds both — legitimately — because he belongs to an order older than Moses\'s law. Jesus holds both offices: He is the Davidic King (Rev. 19:16) AND the eternal High Priest (Heb. 4:14). Only the "order of Melchizedek" makes this possible.
  • No recorded father, mother, genealogy, beginning, or end — Hebrews 7:3 says he is "without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever." God arranged the scriptural record to have deliberate gaps — no birth, no death — making Melchizedek a portrait of One whose priesthood is genuinely without beginning or end: Jesus.
  • He brought bread and wine — the first recorded act of this king-priest is a meal of bread and wine to seal a blessing. At the Last Supper, Jesus — our eternal King-Priest — took bread and wine and said "this is my body... this is my blood" (Matt. 26:26–28). The Lord\'s Supper is the New Covenant Melchizedek meal.
  • Abraham gave him a tenth — the greatest patriarch in Israel\'s history tithed to Melchizedek. The Levitical priests descended from Abraham — so Levi "paid tithes through Abraham" to Melchizedek (Heb. 7:9). Melchizedek\'s order is therefore greater than the Levitical order. Jesus\'s priesthood is greater than the entire Mosaic sacrificial system.
New Testament Connection

Psalm 110:4 — "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek." Hebrews 5:6, 10; 6:20; 7:1–28 — three chapters on Jesus and Melchizedek. Hebrews 7:25 — "He always lives to make intercession for them." Hebrews 7:27 — unlike Levitical priests, Jesus offered Himself once for all. Matthew 26:26–28 — the Last Supper as the new Melchizedek meal.

For Little Ones

"Melchizedek is one of the most mysterious people in the Bible. He just appears — no mom, no dad, no story of how he was born, no story of how he died. He was a king AND a priest at the same time, and he brought bread and wine. Does bread and wine remind you of anything? The Lord's Supper! God put Melchizedek in the Bible as a big clue about Jesus — who is also a King and a Priest forever, and who gives us bread and wine at His table."

Family Discussion
  1. Melchizedek has no recorded beginning or ending in the Bible. Why do you think God arranged the record that way? What was He trying to show us about Jesus?
  2. Melchizedek brought bread and wine to bless Abraham. Jesus took bread and wine at the Last Supper to establish the new covenant. What is the connection? What is Jesus saying by using those same elements?
  3. Jesus is our High Priest right now — not just when He died, but alive and interceding for us this moment (Heb. 7:25). What does it mean for your prayer life to know Jesus is actively praying for you before the Father?
Memory Verse
"Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them."
Hebrews 7:25

Genesis 15 · The Blood Covenant — God Walks Through the Pieces Alone

Genesis 15:1–21
God Walks Through the Pieces — The Covenant of Grace
▼
The Big Idea

In the ancient world, both parties walked between cut animals to seal a covenant — meaning "may this happen to me if I break my promise." In Genesis 15, God put Abraham to sleep and walked through alone. He took both sides of the oath — because He knew Abraham could not keep his end.

📖 What the Verse Says

God tells Abram: "I am your shield; your reward shall be very great." Abram questions — he is still childless. God takes him outside and shows him the stars: "So shall your offspring be." "And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (15:6 — the first explicit statement of justification by faith in the Bible). Then God makes a covenant. He tells Abram to cut animals and lay them in two rows. In covenant-making practice throughout the ancient Near East, both parties would walk between the cut pieces, saying in effect: "May I become like these animals if I break this covenant." Abram falls into a deep sleep. And in the darkness, "a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces" — God, alone, walked through the pieces. Abram never walked. God took both sides of the oath.

🔍 Jesus and the One-Sided Covenant

This is one of the most profound passages in the entire Old Testament. God was essentially saying: "I will keep this covenant. And if it is ever broken — if the penalty ever falls — I will absorb it myself." Abraham never walked. Abraham was asleep. He was passive, unconscious — unable to contribute anything to the covenant-making. The entire covenant rested on God's faithfulness, not Abraham's.

This is grace in its purest form. And this is the cross. At Calvary, the penalty for the broken covenant fell — and God absorbed it in the person of Jesus. The "smoking fire pot and flaming torch" that passed through the pieces is God committing Himself to bear the penalty. Jesus on the cross is that commitment executed — God walking through the pieces alone, bearing the death, keeping the promise.

Genesis 15:6 — "he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness" — is quoted four times in the New Testament (Romans 4:3, 9, 22; Galatians 3:6; James 2:23) as the founding text for the doctrine of justification by faith. Abraham did nothing but believe — and God counted that faith as righteousness. This is the gospel in seed form, 2,000 years before Jesus.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • Abraham's deep sleep (tardemah, 15:12) — the same word used in Genesis 2:21 when Adam was put to sleep before Eve was formed. God does His most significant saving work while His people are passive. We cannot cooperate with grace — we can only receive it.
  • The smoking fire pot and flaming torch — fire represents the presence of God throughout Scripture (the burning bush, Exod. 3:2; the pillar of fire, Exod. 13:21; Pentecost tongues of fire, Acts 2:3). God's presence walked through the pieces — He was physically present in the covenant-making, personally committing Himself.
  • The specific animals (15:9) — a heifer, a goat, a ram (all three years old), a turtledove, and a young pigeon. These exact animals would later appear as the required offerings of the Levitical system. The covenant of Genesis 15 is the prototype; the Levitical sacrifices are the ongoing enactment; and Jesus is the final fulfillment.
New Testament Connection

Romans 4:3, 9, 22 — Genesis 15:6 as the foundation of justification by faith. Galatians 3:6–9 — Abraham's faith is the pattern for all who are justified. Hebrews 6:13–18 — God swore by Himself, because there was no one greater to swear by — the ultimate guarantee. Hebrews 9:15–22 — Jesus as the mediator of a better covenant, sealed with His own blood rather than animal blood.

For Little Ones

"In the old days, when two people made a very serious promise, they would kill animals and walk between them, saying 'If I break this promise, may this happen to me.' In Genesis 15, God told Abraham to set up the animals — but then put Abraham to SLEEP. While Abraham was asleep, God walked through the pieces ALONE. He was saying: 'I promise — and if this promise ever gets broken, I'll take the punishment.' And that's what happened at the cross — God kept His promise by taking the punishment Himself."

Family Discussion
  1. Abraham was asleep when God made the covenant. He contributed nothing to it. What does that tell us about the nature of our salvation — how much is God's doing versus ours?
  2. Genesis 15:6 says Abraham "believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness." Not "he obeyed God" or "he performed the right rituals" — he believed. What is the difference between faith and works? Why does God count faith as righteousness?
  3. God essentially said at Genesis 15: "If this covenant is ever broken, I'll bear the penalty." At the cross, that happened. How does understanding this make the crucifixion feel different — not as a tragedy, but as God keeping His ancient oath?
Memory Verse
"And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness."
Genesis 15:6

Genesis 16 · Hagar — The God Who Sees the Outcast

Genesis 16:1–16
El Roi — "You Are a God Who Sees Me"
▼
The Big Idea

Hagar was a slave, an outsider, mistreated and driven into the wilderness — and the God of Abraham met her there personally. This is the God Jesus reveals: the One who sees the overlooked.

📖 What the Verse Says

Sarai, still waiting for the promised child, offers her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a surrogate. Hagar conceives. Hagar despises Sarai. Sarai mistreats Hagar. Hagar flees into the wilderness alone. The angel of the LORD finds her by a spring in the desert and asks, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" He promises that her son Ishmael will be a great nation. Hagar names the well "Beer-lahai-roi" and gives God a name: "You are a God of seeing... Truly here I have seen him who looks after me." The LORD is given a name by a runaway slave in the desert: El Roi — the God who sees.

🔍 Jesus and El Roi

Hagar was everything the world would have overlooked: a slave, a woman, a foreigner (Egyptian), now a runaway. And the God of the covenant sought her out personally. This is the character of Jesus throughout the Gospels — He consistently sought the ones that the religious establishment overlooked or rejected.
