The woman at the well (John 4 — also a woman, alone, in an outcast situation at a well). The woman caught in adultery (John 8). The lepers, the tax collectors, the children being pushed aside. Jesus is El Roi — the God who sees — and He sees the ones others don't bother to look at.

The "angel of the LORD" who meets Hagar is widely understood by theologians to be a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus Christ — a Christophany. The same figure appears throughout Genesis and Exodus doing things only God can do (forgiving sin, receiving worship) while also appearing in human form. If this is Jesus appearing to Hagar before the incarnation, then the eternal Son of God went out of His way — into the wilderness — to seek a slave woman whom everyone had given up on. That same intentionality is the heart of His ministry: the Good Shepherd who leaves the 99 to find the 1 (Luke 15:4).

New Testament Connection

John 4:7–26 — Jesus at the well with the Samaritan woman (outcast, alone at a well, like Hagar). Luke 15:4 — the Good Shepherd seeking the lost one. Galatians 4:21–31 — Paul uses Hagar and Sarah as an allegory of law vs. grace. Matthew 18:12–14 — God's will is that not one of the little ones be lost.

For Little Ones

"Hagar was all alone in the desert. Nobody cared about her. But God found her! He called her by name. He knew exactly where she was and what she was going through. And she gave God a name: 'The God who sees me.' Jesus is that same God — He sees you. Even when you feel alone or like nobody notices you, Jesus notices. He sees you right now."

Family Discussion
  1. Hagar called God "the God who sees me." Have you ever had a moment where you felt truly seen by God — where it was clear He knew your situation and cared? Share that.
  2. The angel of the LORD went into the wilderness to find one runaway slave. What does that kind of pursuit tell us about how God values people that society ignores or dismisses?
  3. Jesus consistently sought out the overlooked — women, lepers, tax collectors, children. Who are the "Hagars" in your community — the people others don't bother to see? How does El Roi call His people to respond?
Memory Verse
"Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father... Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows."
Matthew 10:29–31

Genesis 17 · The Covenant of Circumcision — The Sign and Its Fulfillment

Genesis 17:1–14
Circumcision — The Sign That Points to Heart Transformation
▼
The Big Idea

Circumcision was always meant to be an outward sign of an inward reality — the cutting away of the flesh, the death of self-reliance, and belonging to God. Jesus is where that inward reality fully arrives.

📖 What the Verse Says

God appears to Abram (now renamed Abraham — "father of many nations") and establishes the covenant of circumcision. "Every male among you shall be circumcised... It shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you." Every male descendant was to bear this physical mark in their flesh. The sign was to be applied on the eighth day.

🔍 What Circumcision Was Always Pointing To

Deuteronomy 10:16 — God told Israel: "Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn." Deuteronomy 30:6 — "And the LORD your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you will love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, that you may live." From very early in Israel's history, God made clear: the physical sign was always a pointer to an inward reality — the transformation of the heart. The outer cutting pointed to an inner cutting away of sin and self-reliance.

Colossians 2:11–12 — Paul says believers receive "a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, buried with him in baptism." Jesus fulfilled the circumcision. His death and resurrection is the true circumcision — the complete cutting away of the old nature, the burial of the flesh. Baptism is the New Covenant circumcision — the sign of belonging to Christ, of the flesh having been cut away, of new life beginning.

The eighth day — circumcision was performed on the eighth day of a male child's life. Eight is the resurrection number (Jesus rose on the eighth day — the day after the Sabbath). Circumcision on the eighth day was always a resurrection sign — death to the old self, new beginning.

New Testament Connection

Colossians 2:11–12 — the true circumcision is in Christ, through burial with Him in baptism. Romans 2:28–29 — "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit." Romans 4:11 — circumcision was "a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised" — faith came first, the sign second. Philippians 3:3 — "we are the circumcision, who worship by the Spirit of God."

For Little Ones

"God gave Abraham's family a special mark to show they belonged to Him. Every baby boy got this mark when they were eight days old. But God always said the most important thing wasn't the mark on the outside — it was the change on the INSIDE. And that's what Jesus does — He changes us on the inside. When we belong to Jesus, it's like God puts His mark on our heart."

Family Discussion
  1. God said the outward sign of circumcision was pointing to "circumcision of the heart." What does a circumcised heart — a heart where the stubbornness and self-reliance has been cut away — actually look like in daily life?
  2. Romans 4:11 says Abraham had the righteousness of faith BEFORE he received the sign of circumcision. What does that tell us about the relationship between faith and outward religious signs or rituals?
  3. Paul says believers are "the circumcision" — those who have received the inward reality the sign always pointed to. What difference does it make in how you live to know you belong to God, marked by Him?
Memory Verse
"For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit."
Romans 2:28–29

Genesis 18–19 · Abraham Intercedes for Sodom — A Portrait of Intercession

Genesis 18:16–33
Abraham's Intercession — The Friend Who Stands in the Gap
▼
The Big Idea

Abraham standing before God pleading for guilty sinners is one of the most powerful pictures of intercession in the Bible — and it points directly to Jesus who always lives to intercede for us.

📖 What the Verse Says

God reveals to Abraham His plan to judge Sodom. Abraham "drew near" and began to intercede — asking whether God would spare the city for 50 righteous, then 45, then 40, then 30, then 20, then 10. Each time, God agrees. "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?" Abraham is standing in the gap — not for himself, but for others. He is appealing to God's character: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" And God listens. The intercession is heard. (Sodom is destroyed because not even 10 righteous were found — but the intercession saved Lot.)

🔍 Jesus — The Perfect Intercessor

Hebrews 7:25 — "He always lives to make intercession for them." Hebrews 9:24 — "Christ has entered... into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf." Romans 8:34 — "Christ Jesus is the one who died — more than that, who was raised — who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us." Jesus is not merely Abraham-like in His intercession. He is the perfect intercessor — and He intercedes not just with words but with His blood. His very wounds are His intercession: the marks of the cross presented before the Father as the evidence of payment made.

Abraham asked "will you spare the city for 50?" counting down to 10. Jesus doesn't count. He says: "I have paid the price for all who come to me." Abraham's intercession was limited by the righteousness of the city's inhabitants. Jesus's intercession is limited only by the willingness of people to come to Him. "He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him" (Heb. 7:25). Uttermost — to the farthest reaches of sin and guilt.

New Testament Connection

Hebrews 7:25 — Jesus's permanent intercession. Romans 8:34 — Jesus interceding at God's right hand. John 17 — Jesus's High Priestly prayer — the greatest intercession in Scripture. 1 John 2:1 — "we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous."

For Little Ones

"Abraham talked to God and said 'please, please don't destroy the city if there are good people there.' He kept asking — 50, 45, 40, 30, 20, 10 — he was begging God to have mercy. That's called intercession — praying for others. Jesus does that for us, every single day. He is talking to His Father about us right now. And because He died for us, His prayer is even more powerful than Abraham's."

Family Discussion
  1. Abraham "drew near" to God to intercede. What does it tell us about our relationship with God that we are invited to "draw near" and bring our requests to Him?
  2. Jesus intercedes for us with His own wounds — the marks of the cross — as the evidence of payment. What does it mean to you that your advocate before the Father bears the marks of what He did for you?
  3. Abraham interceded for sinful people he loved. Who are you interceding for — praying persistently for people who don't yet know Jesus? What would Abraham-like persistence in prayer for others look like?
Memory Verse
"My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous."
1 John 2:1

Genesis 20–21 · The Birth of Isaac — The Son of Promise

Genesis 21:1–7
The Impossible Birth — The Son Who Was Promised
▼
The Big Idea

Isaac was born to a barren woman past the age of childbearing — a supernatural birth that anticipated the even more supernatural birth of Jesus, the ultimate Son of Promise.

📖 What the Verse Says

"The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised. And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him." Abraham was 100 years old. Sarah was 90 and had been barren her entire life. The birth of Isaac was biologically impossible — and it happened exactly as God promised, at exactly the time God had specified. Sarah laughed — "God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me."

🔍 Isaac and Jesus — Sons of Promise

Galatians 4:28 — "Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise." Paul draws a direct line: Isaac's birth was supernatural, promised, and not the result of human effort or natural ability. Jesus's birth was even more so: born of a virgin (Isa. 7:14; Luke 1:35), conceived by the Holy Spirit, announced by an angel — the ultimate fulfillment of the pattern established in Isaac. Both births were impossible by natural means. Both were the direct result of God keeping His word at exactly the right time.

Romans 4:17–21 — Paul uses Abraham and Sarah's faith in the impossible birth as the model for faith in the resurrection. "He gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist." The God who gave life to a dead womb (Sarah's) is the God who raised Jesus from the dead. The faith that believes in impossible births is the same faith that believes in resurrection.

Isaac's name means "laughter" — joy at the impossible made possible. Luke 2:10 — the angel announced the birth of Jesus with "good news of great joy." The same joy that erupted at Isaac's impossible birth erupts again at the birth of the Son of Promise Himself.

New Testament Connection

Galatians 4:28 — believers are children of promise like Isaac. Romans 4:17–22 — faith in the impossible birth as a model for resurrection faith. Hebrews 11:11–12 — Sarah's faith commended. Luke 1:37 — "nothing will be impossible with God" — said at the announcement of Jesus's birth, echoing Isaac's. Luke 1:14 — "great joy" at Jesus's birth, like "laughter" (Isaac) at his.

For Little Ones

"Sarah was way too old to have a baby — everyone knew that. But God had promised. And when Isaac was finally born, Sarah laughed — but a happy laugh! 'I can't believe it! God did the impossible!' That's what the angel said when Jesus was going to be born too: 'Nothing is impossible with God.' God loves doing the impossible. He did it for Isaac. He did it for Mary. And He does it for us when He changes our hearts — that's impossible too, without Him."

Family Discussion
  1. Sarah laughed at God's promise — partly in disbelief (Gen. 18:12) and then in joy (Gen. 21:6). Have you ever moved from "that's impossible" to "God actually did it"? Share that experience.
  2. Both Isaac's birth and Jesus's birth were humanly impossible. Why do you think God arranged the fulfillment of His promises to be humanly impossible — so that only He could get the credit?
  3. Paul says Abraham "did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead" (Rom. 4:19). What does it look like to trust God's promises when all the circumstances say "impossible"?
Memory Verse
"For nothing will be impossible with God."
Luke 1:37

Genesis 22 · The Binding of Isaac — The Most Detailed Picture of the Cross

Genesis 22:1–19
Every Detail of the Binding Points to Calvary
▼
The Big Idea

Genesis 22 is the most concentrated, detailed, verse-by-verse prophecy of the crucifixion in all of Scripture — written two thousand years before it happened.

📖 What the Verse Says

God commands Abraham: "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you." Abraham rises early, saddles his donkey, cuts wood, and takes Isaac and two servants. On the third day he sees the place. He leaves the servants: "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you." Isaac carries the wood. On the way up, Isaac asks: "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham answers: "God will provide for himself the lamb, my son." They arrive. Abraham builds the altar. He binds Isaac. He lays him on the altar. He raises the knife. The angel of the LORD calls out: "Do not lay your hand on the boy!" Abraham looks up — a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. He offers it instead of his son. He names the place: "The LORD will provide." The covenant promises are renewed.

🔍 Verse-by-Verse to Jesus

  • "Your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love" (v.2) — Matthew 3:17: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." Romans 8:32: "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all." The language of Genesis 22:2 and Matthew 3:17 is identical — "only son," "whom you love." God described what Abraham was being asked to do with the exact words He would use of His own Son's sacrifice.
  • "The land of Moriah" (v.2) — 2 Chronicles 3:1: "Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah." This is Jerusalem. This is the Temple Mount. Jesus was crucified in this same mountain range — outside the city walls of Jerusalem, in the same region where Abraham raised the knife over Isaac two thousand years earlier. The cross happened on the mountain where God first announced He would provide a lamb.
  • "On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar" (v.4) — for three days, Isaac was as good as dead in Abraham's mind and heart. Hebrews 11:19: "He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back." Three days. Death. Resurrection. This is the resurrection pattern embedded in Genesis 22.
  • "Stay here... I and the boy will go over there and worship and COME AGAIN TO YOU" (v.5) — Abraham told the servants "we will come back." Both of them. He said this before the sacrifice. This is resurrection faith — Abraham believed God would raise Isaac if he killed him. He went up the mountain expecting to come back down with his son alive. And he did.
  • "Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son" (v.6) — the son carried the wood of the sacrifice up the mountain on his back. John 19:17: "He went out, bearing his own cross." Jesus carried the instrument of His own death up to the place of execution — just as Isaac carried the wood up the mountain.
  • "Where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" (v.7) — this is the question the entire Old Testament is asking. Every Passover, every sacrifice, every burnt offering — they are all variations of this question. The answer comes 2,000 years later: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29). Isaac's question is answered by John the Baptist.
  • "God will provide for himself the lamb, my son" (v.8) — this is a double prophecy. Abraham meant "God will provide a lamb" — and God did. But the deeper meaning is "God will provide HIMSELF as the lamb." Jesus is God providing Himself. The Father offered His own Son. The Son offered Himself. God did not merely send a substitute — He IS the substitute.
  • Isaac's willing submission — Isaac was likely in his late teens or twenties — fully capable of resisting a 100-year-old man. He submitted willingly. John 10:18: "No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord." Both sons submitted voluntarily to their fathers' will.
  • "A ram, caught in a thicket by his horns" (v.13) — a thorn thicket. The ram's head was trapped in thorns. At the crucifixion, the soldiers wove a crown of thorns and pressed it onto Jesus's head (Matt. 27:29). The ram's head caught in thorns — the substitute's head in a crown of thorns. The one who died in Isaac's place had his head in thorns; the One who died in our place had thorns on His head.
  • "The LORD will provide" — Yahweh-Jireh (v.14) — on this mountain God will provide. "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided." Thousands of years later, on this mountain range, God provided His Son — the ultimate Lamb, the final provision, the eternal atonement.
"He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?"Romans 8:32
New Testament Connection

John 1:29 — "Behold, the Lamb of God" — the answer to "where is the lamb?" Romans 8:32 — God "did not spare his own Son" echoes Genesis 22:16. Hebrews 11:17–19 — Abraham's faith included resurrection. John 8:56 — Jesus says Abraham "saw my day" — on Mount Moriah. John 19:17 — Jesus carrying His cross like Isaac carrying wood. Matthew 27:29 — the crown of thorns like the ram caught in thorns.

For Little Ones

Walk through the story slowly and dramatically. Stop at each point: "Isaac carried the wood up the mountain. Who carried something heavy up a hill? Jesus carried His cross. Isaac asked 'where is the lamb?' Who was the Lamb? Jesus! The ram was caught in a crown of thorns. What did Jesus wear? A crown of thorns! God stopped Abraham's hand — but He did NOT stop His own hand when it came to Jesus. Why not? Because He loves us that much."

Family Discussion
  1. Go through the list of parallels. Which one surprises you most? Which one do you think is the most powerful connection?
  2. Abraham said "we will come back" — he believed in resurrection before it had ever happened. Where does that kind of faith come from? How do you get faith like that?
  3. God stopped Abraham from killing Isaac. He did NOT stop Himself from giving His Son. What does that tell you about the depth of God's love for you? What did it cost God to save you?
Memory Verse
"He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?"
Romans 8:32

Genesis 24 · A Bride for the Son — The Spirit Goes to Gather the Church

Genesis 24:1–67
The Servant Sent to Fetch the Bride — A Picture of the Holy Spirit
▼
The Big Idea

Abraham's servant was sent on a mission to find a bride for Isaac — he never speaks of himself, always points to the son, and when the bride agrees to come, he takes her to the son. This is exactly what the Holy Spirit does for Jesus.

📖 What the Verse Says

Abraham, old and near death, sends his oldest servant — unnamed throughout the entire chapter — on the most important mission of his life: go to my homeland and find a wife for my son Isaac. The servant goes with ten camels loaded with gifts. He arrives at a well outside the city of Nahor, prays for a sign, and Rebekah appears — watering the camels, generous and beautiful. The servant gives her gifts. He meets her family, tells the full story of Abraham's wealth, Isaac's inheritance, and the divine guidance that led him here. Rebekah agrees to go. They travel back. Isaac sees the caravan coming, goes to meet them. Rebekah covers herself with a veil. Isaac takes her as his wife and loves her.

🔍 The Servant as the Holy Spirit

This chapter is one of the most overlooked allegories in Genesis — and one of the most profound. The parallels are exact:

  • The Father sends the Servant on a mission — the Father sends the Spirit (John 14:26; 15:26). The Spirit does not come on His own initiative — He is sent.
  • The Servant is never named — throughout all of Genesis 24, the servant is never identified by name. He is always "the servant." The Holy Spirit consistently deflects attention away from Himself and toward Jesus. Jesus said the Spirit "will not speak on his own authority" but "will glorify me" (John 16:13–14). The unnamed servant is a perfect portrait of the Spirit's self-effacing ministry.
  • The Servant brings gifts — he arrives with camels loaded with gifts from Abraham and Isaac. The Spirit comes with gifts — "to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good" (1 Cor. 12:7). The gifts are from the Father and the Son, distributed by the Spirit.
  • The Servant tells the story of the son — in Genesis 24:34–49, the servant tells the full story of Abraham's greatness and Isaac's inheritance. He is not advertising himself — he is presenting the son. This is the Spirit's ministry: He does not come to make much of Himself but to reveal and make much of Jesus (John 16:14).
  • The decision belongs to Rebekah — the family asked her: "Will you go with this man?" And she said: "I will go" (v.58). The Spirit draws and woos — He does not coerce. John 6:44: "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him." The Spirit draws; we respond. Rebekah's willing "I will go" is the response of every soul who says yes to Christ.
  • The Servant brings the Bride to the Son — the servant's entire mission ends when Rebekah is presented to Isaac. John 6:37: "All that the Father gives me will come to me." The Spirit's entire ministry culminates in presenting the Bride — the Church — to the Son at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:7–9).
  • Isaac went out to meet her (v.63–65) — "Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening. And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, there were camels coming. And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel." Jesus will go out to meet His Bride at His return. 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 — the Lord Himself descends, and we are caught up to meet Him.
New Testament Connection

John 14:26; 15:26; 16:13–14 — the Spirit sent by the Father, pointing to Jesus. 1 Corinthians 12:7–11 — gifts distributed by the Spirit. Revelation 19:7–9 — the marriage supper of the Lamb. Revelation 22:17 — "The Spirit and the Bride say, 'Come.'" 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 — Jesus coming to meet His Bride.

For Little Ones

"Abraham sent his servant to find a wife for his son Isaac. The servant's whole job was to find her, tell her about Isaac, and bring her to him. The servant never talked about himself — it was always about Isaac! That's what the Holy Spirit does for Jesus. The Spirit tells us about Jesus, gives us gifts from Jesus, and brings us to Jesus. The Spirit's job is to point us to Jesus — not to make us think about the Spirit himself."

Family Discussion
  1. The servant was never named — his whole identity was "the servant." He only pointed to the son. What does it tell us about the Spirit's ministry that He consistently points away from Himself and toward Jesus?
  2. Rebekah was asked "Will you go?" and she chose to go. How does the Spirit's role in bringing people to Jesus work — does He force anyone, or does He invite and draw? What does that tell us about God's respect for human choice?
  3. The servant's mission ended when Rebekah was presented to Isaac. The Spirit's mission ends at the Marriage Supper of the Lamb. What does it mean that the Holy Spirit's ultimate goal is to bring the Church to Jesus?
Memory Verse
"The Spirit and the Bride say, 'Come.' And let the one who hears say, 'Come.' And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price."
Revelation 22:17

Genesis 25–26 · Jacob and Esau — Grace That Overturns Expectation

Genesis 25:19–34
"The Older Will Serve the Younger" — Grace Reverses Human Order
▼
The Big Idea

God choosing Jacob over Esau — before either was born, before either had done anything — is the most radical statement of sovereign grace in Genesis. Paul uses it to teach the doctrine of election in Romans 9.

📖 What the Verse Says

Rebekah is pregnant with twins and they struggle within her. She asks God what is happening. God says: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger." Jacob and Esau are born. Esau, the firstborn, is the expected heir. Jacob is the second. But God has already declared: the younger will receive the promise. This reversal of the expected order appears throughout Scripture and always points to the same truth: God's grace does not follow human logic or human hierarchy.

🔍 The Pattern of Grace Through the Unexpected

Romans 9:10–13 — Paul quotes Genesis 25 directly: "Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls — she was told, 'The older will serve the younger.'" Paul uses Jacob and Esau to explain the freedom of God's grace — it does not operate on the basis of human merit, birth order, or expected privilege. It operates on the basis of God's sovereign choice and call.

This pattern repeats constantly through Genesis and Scripture as a whole: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Ephraim over Manasseh, David over his older brothers. God consistently bypasses the expected, the firstborn, the obvious choice — to show that His gifts are not earned. They are given. This is the gospel: "Not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Tim. 1:9). Our salvation, like Jacob's election, was determined before we had done anything to earn it.

New Testament Connection

Romans 9:10–13 — Jacob and Esau as the illustration of sovereign grace and election. 2 Timothy 1:9 — grace given before the ages began. Ephesians 1:4–5 — chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world. 1 Corinthians 1:27–29 — God chooses the weak and despised to shame the strong.

For Little Ones

"God said 'the older will serve the younger' before Jacob and Esau were even born! Neither had done anything yet. God chose Jacob because He wanted to — not because Jacob was better. That's what grace means. And Paul quotes this in Romans 9 to explain how God saves us: not because of anything we did, but because of His own choice and love. Salvation has always been God's idea, not ours."

Family Discussion
  1. God chose Jacob before Jacob had done anything. Does that seem fair? What does it tell us about how God's choices work — are they based on what we do, or on something else?
  2. Paul says Jacob and Esau are an example of God's sovereign grace in salvation. What does it mean that your salvation was planned before you were born? How does that make you feel?
  3. God consistently chooses the unexpected person — the younger, the weaker, the outsider. Why do you think He works this way? What does it accomplish that choosing the "obvious" candidate would not?
Memory Verse
"He saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began."
2 Timothy 1:9

Genesis 27–28 · Jacob's Ladder — The Bridge Between Heaven and Earth

Genesis 28:10–22
The Stairway to Heaven — Jesus Is the Only Way Up
▼
The Big Idea

Jacob dreamed of a staircase connecting heaven and earth with angels ascending and descending on it — and Jesus said "I am that staircase."

📖 What the Verse Says

Jacob, fleeing from Esau, stops for the night in the wilderness and dreams. He sees "a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it! And behold, the LORD stood above it" — and renewed the Abrahamic covenant to Jacob. Jacob woke in awe: "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." He set up the stone he had been using as a pillow, anointed it with oil, and called the place Bethel — "house of God."

🔍 Jesus Claimed to BE the Ladder

John 1:51 — Jesus said to Nathanael: "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man." This is a direct, deliberate reference to Genesis 28. Jesus identifies Himself as the ladder in Jacob's dream. He IS the connection between heaven and earth — the only meeting point of the divine and human realms.

Jacob called the place "the gate of heaven." Jesus said "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). He is the gate of heaven — not a gate, not one gate among many — THE gate. Jacob's "gate of heaven" was a specific, geographic location where God met him. Jesus is the gate of heaven for every person and every place — the universal, permanent, living connection between God and humanity.

Jacob anointed the stone with oil — mashach in Hebrew, the root of "Messiah" (Anointed One). The anointed stone set up as a pillar at Bethel points to Jesus — the Anointed One, the cornerstone (Eph. 2:20; 1 Pet. 2:6–7), set up as the foundation of God's house (the Church).

New Testament Connection

John 1:51 — Jesus as the ladder, explicitly stated. John 14:6 — "I am the way" — the only path between God and humanity. 1 Timothy 2:5 — "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Ephesians 2:20 — Jesus as the cornerstone of God's house. Hebrews 4:16 — we can draw near to the throne of grace — because the ladder exists.

For Little Ones

"Jacob dreamed of a staircase going from the ground all the way up to heaven, with angels going up and down. Wouldn't that be amazing to see? Now here's the best part — Jesus said to His friends: 'I am that staircase!' Jesus connects us to God. Without Jesus, there is no way to get from where we are to where God is. With Jesus, the way is open. He is the staircase — and we can always climb."

Family Discussion
  1. Jacob stumbled onto this place — he didn't know it was special before he got there. Have you ever had a moment where you encountered God in an unexpected place? What was that like?
  2. Jesus said "I am the ladder" — not "I show you the ladder" or "I point to the ladder." He IS the connection. What does it mean that Jesus himself is the bridge between heaven and earth, not just someone who explains how to get there?
  3. "No one comes to the Father except through me" — this is one of the most exclusive statements Jesus ever made. Is that offensive or comforting to you? What does the exclusivity of Jesus as "the way" mean for how we share our faith with others?
Memory Verse
"Jesus said to him, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.'"
John 14:6

Genesis 32–33 · Jacob Wrestling God — The Man Who Would Not Let Go

Genesis 32:22–32
Wrestling With God — The Christophany at the Jabbok
▼
The Big Idea

Jacob wrestled with a Man who turned out to be God — and walked away with a limp and a new name. This is one of the most mysterious encounters in Genesis, and it is almost certainly a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus Christ.

📖 What the Verse Says

Jacob, alone at night before his terrifying reunion with Esau, "wrestled with a man until the breaking of the day." The man could not overcome Jacob — so he touched his hip socket and put it out of joint. He asked Jacob to let him go. Jacob: "I will not let you go unless you bless me." The man asked his name. "Jacob." "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed." Jacob asked the man's name — and He refused to give it, but blessed Jacob there. Jacob named the place Peniel: "For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered."

🔍 Jesus in the Wrestling Match

Who was this "man"? Hosea 12:3–5 interprets the passage: Jacob "strove with God. He strove with the angel and prevailed." The Man is both God and Angel — the Angel of the LORD, the pre-incarnate Christ. He appears in human form (taking on flesh before the permanent incarnation), wrestles with Jacob, touches him with supernatural power, blesses him, and gives him a new name. This is exactly what Jesus does — He comes to us in the form of a man, He engages our resistance, He wounds us (the limp that produces dependence), He blesses us, and He gives us a new identity (2 Cor. 5:17).

The limp Jacob received was not a punishment — it was a gift. It was the physical mark of his encounter with God. It meant every step for the rest of his life was a reminder that he had met God and lived. And it turned him from a self-reliant schemer (Jacob = "he grasps the heel" / deceiver) into a man who walked with a limp and depended on God. The wound that produces dependence is a feature of grace, not a punishment. Paul received a "thorn in the flesh" for the same purpose (2 Cor. 12:7–9). God sometimes wounds us to keep us leaning on Him.

🔍 "I Will Not Let You Go Unless You Bless Me"

This is the posture of persevering prayer — of faith that will not release God until blessing comes. Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8) to teach exactly this: persistence in prayer that does not give up. Jacob's wrestling is the Old Testament portrait of the prayer Jesus calls for — not passive resignation, but active, persistent, even desperate engagement with God that refuses to quit until the blessing arrives.

New Testament Connection

Hosea 12:3–5 — the wrestler was "the angel" and God. 2 Corinthians 12:7–9 — Paul's thorn in the flesh producing dependence, like Jacob's limp. Luke 18:1–8 — the persistent widow as the NT form of Jacob's wrestling. 2 Corinthians 5:17 — new name/new identity in Christ. Revelation 2:17 — Jesus gives overcomers a new name, written on a white stone.

For Little Ones

"Jacob spent all night wrestling with God — and he wouldn't let go until God blessed him. God gave him a new name: Israel, which means 'he struggles with God.' The whole nation of God's people is named after a wrestling match! Jesus said in John 16: 'Ask and you will receive.' Jacob is the picture of persistent, desperate prayer that will not give up. And the wound in Jacob's hip that stayed forever? Wounds from wrestling with God often stay — and become our story of His faithfulness."

Family Discussion
  1. "I will not let you go unless you bless me" — what does this tell us about the right kind of persistence in prayer? What is the difference between demanding God do what we want and the kind of persisting Jacob showed?
  2. Jacob's limp was a permanent reminder of his encounter with God. What "limps" — weakness, scars, areas of dependency — in your life might actually be gifts that keep you leaning on God?
  3. God gave Jacob a new name — Israel. Jesus gives His people a new identity — no longer defined by their past but by who they are in Him. What is your "new name" — the identity Jesus has given you that is truer than your failures?
Memory Verse
"And he said, 'Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.'"
Genesis 32:28

Genesis 37–41 · Joseph: Betrayed, Imprisoned, Exalted

Genesis 37–41
Joseph's Story Part 1 — The Beloved Son Betrayed and Exalted
▼
The Big Idea

Joseph's journey from beloved son to betrayed prisoner to exalted ruler at the right hand of Pharaoh is not just a story of personal triumph. It is a verse-by-verse prophecy of the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

📖 What the Verse Says

Jacob loved Joseph above all his sons and gave him a special robe. Joseph's brothers hated him, conspired to kill him, threw him in a pit, then sold him to traders for twenty pieces of silver. They brought his blood-dipped robe to Jacob. Joseph was taken to Egypt, sold to Potiphar, falsely accused, imprisoned with criminals, interpreted dreams, was forgotten, then remembered when Pharaoh dreamed. He was elevated to Pharaoh's right hand at age thirty. He provided bread for the starving world.

🔍 Verse-by-Verse to Jesus

  • The beloved son (37:3) — Jacob loved Joseph more than any other. At Jesus's baptism: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3:17). Both are the specially beloved, uniquely cherished son of their father.
  • The special robe (37:3) — the robe marked Joseph's special status and was what provoked the brothers' hatred. Jesus's garments were stripped from Him (Matt. 27:28). But He is now clothed in glory (Rev. 1:13).
  • Sent by the father to his brothers (37:13–14) — "Go now, see if it is well with your brothers." Jesus: "The Father has sent me" (John 5:36). Both sent by their father to those who would reject them.
  • Hated without cause (37:4, 8) — they hated him because of his dreams and his father's love. Jesus: "They hated me without a cause" (John 15:25). The righteous are hated not for what they do wrong but for what they represent.
  • Conspired against from a distance (37:18) — "before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him." Matthew 26:3–4 — the chief priests "plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him."
  • The pit (37:24) — "they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it." The pit in the Psalms is the image of Sheol — death. Joseph in the pit is Jesus in the tomb — in the place of the dead.
  • Judah proposes selling him for silver (37:26–28) — Judah (the Greek form is Judas) proposed selling the beloved brother. They sold him for twenty pieces of silver. Judas Iscariot proposed betraying Jesus and received thirty pieces of silver (Matt. 26:15). Both Judah/Judas — same name — betrayed the beloved son for silver.
  • Stripped of his robe (37:23) — stripped before the betrayal. Jesus was stripped of His garments at the crucifixion (Matt. 27:28).
  • Robe dipped in blood — false evidence (37:31) — the brothers brought "evidence" of his death — blood on the robe — to deceive the father. False witnesses testified against Jesus at His trial (Matt. 26:59–60).
  • False accusation (39:14–18) — Potiphar's wife falsely accused him of assault. Jesus was falsely accused by false witnesses at His trial. Both were innocent; both were condemned by lies.
  • Numbered with transgressors — in prison with criminals (39:20) — Joseph was thrown into the prison where the king's prisoners were kept. Jesus was crucified between two criminals. Isaiah 53:12: "he was numbered with the transgressors."
  • The two prisoners — one saved, one not (40:1–23) — in prison with Joseph were the cupbearer and the baker. Joseph interpreted their dreams: the cupbearer would be restored to life in three days; the baker would be executed in three days. This is the two criminals at the cross — one was restored to paradise, one was not (Luke 23:39–43). Three days — death and resurrection — for both Joseph and Jesus.
  • Forgotten and then remembered (40:23; 41:1) — "the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him." Jesus was forsaken and abandoned — but God remembered. Easter Sunday is the ultimate "remembering."
  • Raised up and exalted at age thirty (41:46) — Joseph was thirty years old when Pharaoh elevated him. Jesus "was about thirty years of age" when He began His public ministry (Luke 3:23).
  • Exalted to the right hand of power (41:40–43) — Pharaoh made Joseph second in command — his right hand. "Jesus has been exalted to the right hand of God" (Acts 2:33).
  • "Every knee shall bow" (41:43) — every Egyptian bowed before Joseph. "At the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Phil. 2:10).
  • Bread for a starving world (41:56–57) — "all the earth came to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain." Jesus: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger" (John 6:35). The whole world came to Joseph for physical bread; the whole world is invited to come to Jesus for the bread of eternal life.
New Testament Connection

Matthew 26:14–15 — Judas's betrayal of Jesus for silver. Luke 3:23 — Jesus began ministry at thirty. Acts 2:33 — Jesus at the right hand of God. Philippians 2:10 — every knee bowing. John 6:35 — Jesus as the bread of life. Luke 23:39–43 — the two criminals at the cross.

For Little Ones

"Joseph's whole life is a picture of Jesus — written 2,000 years before Jesus was born. Beloved son, rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, falsely accused, thrown into a pit, raised up to save the very people who rejected him. Every detail lines up. When Joseph finally revealed himself to his brothers he said: 'Don't be angry with yourselves — God sent me here to save lives.' That's exactly what Jesus says to us: 'Don't be angry with yourselves — what you did to me, God used to save the world.' Joseph didn't just survive his suffering. He used it to rescue the ones who caused it."

Family Discussion
  1. Which of the Joseph-Jesus parallels surprises you most? Which one do you think is the most powerful or moving?
  2. Joseph was age thirty when he was exalted, and Jesus was thirty when He began His ministry. Why do you think God would embed that kind of specific detail across 2,000 years of history?
  3. The two prisoners with Joseph (one saved, one executed) mirror the two criminals at the cross (one saved, one not). What determines which side you are on — the cupbearer who lived or the baker who died?
Memory Verse
"Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow."
Philippians 2:9–10

Genesis 42–50 · Joseph Reveals Himself and Forgives

Genesis 42–50
The Great Reveal — Tears, Forgiveness, and "God Meant It for Good"
▼
The Big Idea

Joseph's tearful reveal to his brothers — "I am Joseph. Do not be afraid. God meant it for good" — is one of the most powerful pictures of the gospel's grace in the entire Bible. And it points straight to Jesus.

📖 What the Verse Says

The brothers come to Egypt repeatedly for grain. Joseph recognizes them but tests them — not for cruelty, but to see if they have changed. He puts Benjamin (his mother's only other son) at risk to see if they will sacrifice him the way they sacrificed Joseph. When Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place (Gen. 44:33) — the moment of transformation — Joseph can contain himself no longer. He weeps so loudly the Egyptians hear it. He reveals himself: "I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt... do not be distressed or angry with yourselves... for God sent me before you to preserve life." He kisses all his brothers. The family is reunited. When Jacob dies and the brothers fear Joseph will now take revenge, Joseph says: "Do not fear... As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good."

🔍 Jesus in the Reveal

  • Joseph tested his brothers before the reveal (42–44) — Joseph did not reveal himself immediately. He tested them to see if they had changed. God's dealings with us often include testing — not to determine what He does not know, but to reveal what we are made of, and to bring about the transformation that makes the relationship possible. Jesus tested Philip before the feeding of the 5,000 (John 6:6 — "He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do").
  • Judah offered himself as a substitute for Benjamin (44:33) — "please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord." This is the transforming moment — Judah, who had proposed selling Joseph, now offers himself to save another brother. This is the transformation that makes the reveal possible. At the cross, the tribe of Judah (Jesus) offered Himself as a substitute for all of us.
  • "He wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard it" (45:2) — Joseph's weeping was uncontained, explosive, not hidden. Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35). Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). The Savior who was betrayed, who had every right to be cold and formal, wept with love. The gospel is not a cold transaction — it is a tearful, joyful reunion.
  • "I am Joseph" (45:3) — the three words that changed everything. "I am" — the same construction Jesus used in John 8:58: "Before Abraham was, I am." The great "I am" declarations of Jesus (John 6, 8, 10, 11, 14, 15) are always moments of dramatic self-revelation — this is who I am. Receive it or reject it.
  • "Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves" (45:5) — before the brothers could spiral into guilt and shame, Joseph redirected. He did not minimize what they did — but he refused to let guilt destroy the reunion. This is the grace of the gospel: Jesus does not want His redeemed people destroyed by shame. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom. 8:1).
  • "God sent me before you to preserve life" (45:5, 7) — Joseph reframed the entire narrative. What the brothers intended as evil — God intended as salvation. This is the gospel's logic applied to Joseph's story: the darkest chapter became the means of life for everyone. At the cross: what Rome and the Pharisees intended as execution, God intended as the salvation of the world.
  • "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (50:20) — the theological summit of the Joseph narrative. Every betrayal, every pit, every false accusation, every prison year — God was purposing something that human evil was serving without knowing it. Romans 8:28: "We know that for those who love God all things work together for good." This is not optimism — it is theology. God's sovereignty over evil does not excuse the evil (the brothers were genuinely guilty) but it does guarantee that evil never has the final word.
  • Saving both Jews and Gentiles (47:11–12; 41:56–57) — Joseph provided for his own family AND for all the nations who came to buy grain. Jesus came "to the Jew first and also to the Greek" (Rom. 1:16). The salvation Joseph brought was universal; the salvation Jesus brings is for all.
"As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today."Genesis 50:20
New Testament Connection

Romans 8:1 — no condemnation, like Joseph's "do not be distressed." Romans 8:28 — all things work together for good, like Genesis 50:20. Luke 23:34 — "Father, forgive them" — Joseph's forgiveness of his brothers. John 11:35; Luke 19:41 — Jesus weeping, like Joseph weeping. Acts 7:9–14 — Stephen explicitly connects Joseph to Jesus's pattern of rejection and exaltation.

For Little Ones

"When Joseph finally told his brothers who he was, he cried so loudly that everyone heard! He wasn't angry. He was SO happy to see them. He hugged them and kissed them — even though they had been so mean to him. And then he said the most amazing thing: 'Don't be upset. You meant to hurt me — but God meant it to help everyone.' That's what Jesus says about the cross too. People meant it for evil. God meant it for the greatest good in all of history."

Family Discussion
  1. Genesis 50:20 — "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." Can you think of something hard or painful in your own life that God has used for good? What does Genesis 50:20 give you to hold onto in the painful chapters?
  2. Joseph wept when he revealed himself. He wasn't cold or formal — he was emotionally overcome with love. What does that tell us about the heart of Jesus toward those who have wronged Him and then come to Him?
  3. Judah offered himself as a substitute for Benjamin — and that act of sacrifice was the turning point of the whole story. How does substitutionary sacrifice — someone taking another's place — run through the entire Joseph narrative? And through the gospel?
Memory Verse
"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose."
Romans 8:28

Genesis 23 · Sarah's Death & Burial — The Stranger Who Buys Land He Will One Day Own

Genesis 23:1–20
Abraham the Stranger Buys a Burial Place — A Picture of Christ Purchasing Our Inheritance
▼
The Big Idea

Abraham was a stranger in a land God had promised him — he owned none of it yet. When Sarah died, he had to buy a small piece of it. This is a picture of Christ purchasing what already belongs to Him — because love required it.

📖 What the Verse Says

Sarah died at 127 years old in Hebron. Abraham "rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites, 'I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.'" The Hittites offered to give him any tomb he chose. But Abraham insisted on purchasing — not receiving as a gift — the cave of Machpelah from Ephron, for four hundred shekels of silver, the full commercial price. He bought it publicly, at the city gate, with witnesses. He owned that field and that cave from that day on — a small piece of the land God had promised him.

🔍 How This Points to Jesus

Hebrews 11:13–16 — "These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth." Abraham lived his whole life as a stranger in the land God had promised him. He owned nothing of it — except this one field, purchased with silver, for the sake of love for the one he had lost.

Jesus owns all things — "all things were created through him and for him" (Col. 1:16). The whole earth is His. And yet He "became poor" (2 Cor. 8:9), came as a stranger to His own world ("he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him," John 1:11), and purchased what already belonged to Him — not with silver, but with His own blood. He bought us back not because He had to but because love required it. Abraham did not need to buy Machpelah — the whole land was already his by promise. He bought it because Sarah was there, and love demanded a place for her. Christ did not need to purchase us — the universe is His. He purchased us because we were there, lost, and love demanded our redemption.

The purchase was public — at the city gate, with witnesses, at full price. Jesus's purchase of His people was public — the cross, outside the city, witnessed by the world, at full price. Nothing hidden. Nothing discounted. Full payment.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • "I am a sojourner and foreigner among you" (23:4) — Abraham confessed his status honestly. Jesus, the eternal Son, became a sojourner in His own creation — "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). The word "dwelt" is literally "tabernacled" — pitched a tent. He was a temporary resident of what He owned eternally.
  • Four hundred shekels of silver — full commercial price (23:15–16) — Abraham refused to accept the land as a gift. He paid the full price. Jesus paid the full price — not silver, but "the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet. 1:18–19).
  • The cave of Machpelah became the burial place of the patriarchs — Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were all buried there. It became the family tomb — the deposit of resurrection hope. The grave purchased by Abraham became a container of resurrection promises. Jesus's tomb — also purchased (Joseph of Arimathea's new tomb, Matt. 27:60) — became the site of the first resurrection.
  • Ephesians 1:13–14 — the Holy Spirit is the "guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it." We are still in the "sojourner" phase — we have the promise, the Spirit as a deposit, but not yet the full possession. Like Abraham with Machpelah, we have a purchased piece of the inheritance — the Spirit — while the full promise awaits.
New Testament Connection

Hebrews 11:13–16 — strangers and exiles greeting the promise from afar. 1 Peter 1:18–19 — redeemed not with silver but with the blood of Christ. John 1:11–14 — came to his own, pitched His tent among us. Ephesians 1:13–14 — the Spirit as a deposit guaranteeing the full inheritance. 2 Corinthians 8:9 — though he was rich, he became poor for our sake.

For Little Ones

"Abraham lived his whole life in a land that God had promised him — but he didn't own any of it. He was like a guest in his own house. When Sarah died, he had to BUY a small piece of that land just to bury her — because he loved her. He paid full price. He didn't take it for free. That's what Jesus did for us. The whole universe is His — He made it! But He came as a stranger and bought us back with His own blood because He loves us. He didn't have to. Love made Him do it."

Family Discussion
  1. Abraham paid full price for land that was already his by promise. Jesus paid full price — His life — for people who were already His by creation. What does the insistence on full payment tell us about how God treats love and covenant?
  2. We are still "strangers and foreigners" in this world, like Abraham was. What does that mean practically for how you relate to your possessions, your home, your country?
  3. The Spirit is called a "deposit" guaranteeing our inheritance. Abraham's field was his deposit — the first piece of what would eventually be fully his. What does it mean to you that the Spirit you have right now is just the first installment of something infinitely greater?
Memory Verse
"For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich."
2 Corinthians 8:9

Genesis 26 · Isaac Re-Digs the Wells — Restoring What Was Stopped Up

Genesis 26:12–33
The Wells Stopped Up and Re-Opened — Jesus Restores Access to Living Water
▼
The Big Idea

The Philistines had deliberately stopped up all the wells Abraham had dug. Isaac came back and re-dug every one of them, calling them by the same names his father had given them. This is a picture of what Jesus does — He reopens every source of life that sin and the enemy have stopped up.

📖 What the Verse Says

Isaac settled in Gerar and sowed seed and reaped a hundredfold — the LORD blessed him greatly. The Philistines envied him and "stopped up all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, filling them with earth." Then Isaac "dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham. And he gave them the names that his father had given them." He dug new wells too. Enemies contested them — Esek (contention), Sitnah (enmity). But a third well was uncontested — he called it Rehoboth: "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."

🔍 How This Points to Jesus

The wells of Abraham represent access to God — the sources of living water that God had opened through covenant relationship. The Philistines (enemies of God's people) had deliberately blocked them — filling them with earth, stopping up every source. This is exactly what sin does. Sin stops up every source of life — access to God, joy, peace, meaningful relationship, true identity. What God opens, the enemy works to block.

Isaac came back and re-dug every well — calling them by their fathers' names, honoring what Abraham had established, restoring what had been stopped up. Jesus came to re-dig every well the enemy had blocked. John 4:10 — "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water." At a well — the very symbol of re-dug access to water — Jesus offered the woman of Samaria what no Philistine could ever stop up again: living water welling up to eternal life (John 4:14).

Jesus re-digs the wells of: access to the Father (the veil was torn), joy (John 15:11 — "that my joy may be in you"), peace (John 14:27 — "my peace I give to you"), purpose (Eph. 2:10 — "created in Christ Jesus for good works"), and identity (John 1:12 — "children of God"). Every well the Fall stopped up, Jesus re-opens. And the final well — Rehoboth, "the LORD has made room for us" — is the new creation, where there is room enough for all God's people to be fruitful forever.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • Isaac called the wells by their father's names (26:18) — he honored what Abraham had established. Jesus said "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them" (Matt. 5:17). He honored and fulfilled what the Father had established through Moses, not replacing it with something alien but bringing it to its intended completion.
  • Esek (contention) and Sitnah (enmity) — two contested wells — the enemy contests access to living water. Jesus warned His disciples they would face opposition (John 15:18–20). The enemy contests the wells. But the final well — Rehoboth — is uncontested. In the new creation, there will be no more opposition, no more Philistines to stop up the water.
  • "Now the LORD has made room for us" (26:22) — Rehoboth. Jesus said "In my Father's house are many rooms... I go to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2). The LORD makes room. Always room. For all who come.
  • Isaac sowed and reaped a hundredfold (26:12) — in the midst of famine, God blessed Isaac with an extraordinary harvest. Jesus described the kingdom of God as seed producing thirty, sixty, a hundredfold (Mark 4:8). Abundance in the midst of scarcity is God's signature.
New Testament Connection

John 4:10–14 — Jesus offering living water at a well. Matthew 5:17 — Jesus fulfilling, not abolishing. John 14:2 — "many rooms" in the Father's house. John 7:37–38 — "rivers of living water" flowing from those who believe. Revelation 22:1 — the river of the water of life in the new creation.

For Little Ones

"The enemies of Isaac's family had filled up all the wells with dirt — on purpose! So Isaac went back and dug them all out again, one by one, calling them the same names his dad had given them. Sin does the same thing to us — it fills up all the good things in our lives with dirt and darkness. And Jesus comes and re-digs them. He restores joy, peace, closeness with God, purpose. He makes room for us again. And one day He'll make the biggest room of all — in heaven, where there is room for everyone."

Family Discussion
  1. The Philistines stopped up the wells — deliberately blocking access to water. What are the "wells" in your life that the enemy or sin has tried to stop up — sources of joy, peace, or closeness with God?
  2. Isaac re-dug every well and called them by the same names his father had given them. Jesus restored what the Fall had blocked and honored what the Father had established. What does that tell us about the relationship between the Old Testament and the New?
  3. The third well — Rehoboth — means "the LORD has made room." What does it mean to you that God always makes room? Is there anyone you're afraid might not fit in God's kingdom?
Memory Verse
"Jesus said to her, 'Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again.'"
John 4:13–14

Genesis 29–31 · Jacob Labors for His Bride — The Bridegroom Who Pays Any Price

Genesis 29:1–30
Seven Years That Seemed Like Days — The Love That Drives the Gospel
▼
The Big Idea

Jacob worked seven years for Rachel — and it seemed like only days because of his love. Then he was deceived and had to work seven more years. He paid fourteen years of labor for his bride. Jesus paid with His life for His — and calls it worth it.

📖 What the Verse Says

Jacob arrived at Laban's house, saw Rachel, and loved her. He offered to work seven years for her hand in marriage. "So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her" (29:20). On the wedding night, Laban deceived him — substituting Leah behind the veil. Jacob discovered the deception in the morning. Laban explained the custom of the firstborn marrying first. Jacob worked another seven years — fourteen years total — for the woman he loved.

🔍 How This Points to Jesus

Ephesians 5:25–27 — "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish." Jacob's fourteen years of labor for his bride is a portrait of the infinite cost Christ paid for His. Jacob could have walked away after the deception — but his love for Rachel kept him working. Jesus could have refused the cross — but His love for His Bride kept Him going. Hebrews 12:2 — "For the joy set before him he endured the cross, scorning its shame." The joy was His Bride. The price was His life. And He considered it worth it.

Seven years seemed like days because of love. The eternal Son of God stepped into thirty-three years of human existence — years of rejection, suffering, homelessness, misunderstanding, and ultimately crucifixion — and submitted to it all for the love of His Bride. Time, suffering, cost — all swallowed up by the magnitude of the love.

The deception of Laban — the substitution of Leah for Rachel — is also significant. Jacob received a bride he did not choose, before the bride he loved. Jesus received all of us — in our sin, our brokenness, our deception — before presenting us to Himself as the radiant Bride without spot. He received the Leah of what we were so He could make us the Rachel of what we will be.

🔍 Leah — The Unloved One God Sees

"When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren" (29:31). Leah was unloved by her husband — but deeply seen by God. God turned toward the one everyone else turned away from. Through Leah came Judah — and through Judah came Jesus. The unloved, overlooked woman carried the line of the Messiah. Jesus consistently turned toward the Leahs of the world — the overlooked, the unwanted, the rejected. And He Himself was the ultimate Leah — "despised and rejected by men" (Isa. 53:3) — yet chosen by the Father to be the Savior of the world.

New Testament Connection

Ephesians 5:25–27 — Christ's love for the Church like a husband for his wife. Hebrews 12:2 — the joy set before him, enduring the cross. Isaiah 53:3 — despised and rejected, like Leah. Matthew 1:2–3 — Judah (Leah's son) in the genealogy of Jesus. Revelation 19:7–9 — the Marriage Supper of the Lamb.

For Little Ones

"Jacob loved Rachel so much that he worked for seven years to marry her — and the Bible says it felt like just a few days because he loved her so much. Then he got tricked and had to work SEVEN MORE years! Fourteen years total. But his love for Rachel kept him going. Jesus loves His people — the Church, all who trust in Him — like that. He went through everything — the cross, the suffering, the darkness — because of His love. And He says it was worth it. That's how much He loves you."

Family Discussion
  1. "Seven years seemed like only days because of his love." Have you ever worked hard or suffered for something or someone you loved deeply, and found the cost easier because of the love? How does that help you understand the cross?
  2. God saw Leah when Jacob didn't. Who are the "Leahs" in your life — the people everyone else overlooks? How does God's response to Leah shape how you should respond to them?
  3. Leah, the unloved one, carried the line of the Messiah. What does it tell you about God that He chose to bring Jesus into the world through the rejected, overlooked woman rather than the beloved, chosen one?
Memory Verse
"...looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God."
Hebrews 12:2

Genesis 34 · Dinah — God's Response to Violation and Injustice

Genesis 34:1–31
The Darkest Chapter — and What It Reveals About God's Justice
▼
The Big Idea

Genesis 34 is one of the Bible's darkest chapters — sexual violence, revenge, deception, and mass killing. It is in the Bible because God does not look away from evil. And it points to Jesus as the only one who can bring true justice without becoming the very thing He fights against.

📖 What the Verse Says

Dinah, Jacob's daughter, went out to visit the women of the land. Shechem, son of the local ruler, saw her, seized her, and raped her. Then he fell in "love" with her and wanted to marry her. His father negotiated with Jacob. Her brothers, Simeon and Levi, deceived the Shechemites into circumcision, then — while they were recovering — killed all the males of the city and plundered everything. Jacob rebuked them: "You have brought trouble on me by making me stink to the inhabitants of the land." They answered: "Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?"

🔍 How This Points to Jesus

This chapter is often skipped because it is uncomfortable. But that is exactly why it is here. The Bible does not sanitize human evil. It records it honestly — and places it in the context of God's ongoing work in a broken family, in a broken world, on the way to a Savior.

God sees Dinah. Her name means "justice" or "judgment." She is violated and her voice is almost entirely absent from the narrative — her brothers speak, her father speaks, Shechem speaks. But God sees her. The God who saw Hagar in the wilderness (Gen. 16) sees Dinah in her violation. Jesus, who stopped for the bleeding woman (Mark 5), who protected the woman caught in adultery (John 8), who spoke directly to the Samaritan woman (John 4) — He is the God who sees and stops for women that the world treats as invisible or disposable.

Simeon and Levi's revenge was understandable — but it became worse than the original evil. They used the holy covenant sign of circumcision as a weapon of deception. They turned something sacred into something violent. Their anger was not wrong — sin demands a response. But their method was corrupt. This is the fundamental human problem with justice: we cannot execute it without becoming corrupt in the process. Romans 12:19 — "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." Only God can execute perfect justice without corruption. Jesus is the only judge who can condemn sin without becoming sinful in the condemning.

Jesus is the answer to Genesis 34. He is the one who will bring true justice — not Simeon and Levi's revenge, but the perfect, holy, incorruptible justice of God. Revelation 19:11 — "He judges and makes war" in righteousness. Every Dinah — every violated, unseen, unheard sufferer — is seen by God, and the account will be settled perfectly by the One who died for sinners and will judge sin in righteousness.

🔍 Details That Point to Jesus

  • Circumcision used as a weapon (34:13–17) — the covenant sign of belonging to God was weaponized by Jacob's sons. Jesus's cross — the ultimate act of self-giving — is also sometimes weaponized by people as a tool of religious coercion or manipulation. But the cross itself remains pure. The sign of the covenant, like circumcision, is holy regardless of how people misuse it.
  • Jacob's silence (34:5) — Jacob heard what happened and "held his peace until they came." His silence in the face of his daughter's violation is one of the most painful moments in Genesis. God is not silent. He sees every act of violence against the vulnerable and will not hold His peace forever (Ps. 10:17–18).
  • Simeon and Levi's descendants — because of this act, Simeon's tribe eventually lost its territory and was absorbed into Judah. Levi's tribe was scattered — but in a different way: they became the priestly tribe, scattered throughout Israel to serve God. The same event that brought judgment on Simeon brought a different kind of scattering on Levi — one that ultimately served God's redemptive purpose. Even in this dark chapter, God was working.
New Testament Connection

Romans 12:19 — "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." Revelation 19:11 — Jesus judging in righteousness. John 8:1–11 — Jesus protecting the violated and condemned woman. Mark 5:25–34 — Jesus stopping for the unseen suffering woman. Psalm 10:17–18 — God hearing the cry of the afflicted.

For Little Ones

"This is one of the hardest chapters in Genesis — something very wrong happened to someone, and then more wrong things happened as people tried to fix it. It's in the Bible to show us that God doesn't pretend bad things don't happen. He sees them. He cares. And He promises that one day Jesus will make everything right — perfectly right, in a way that people never can. Jesus is the only judge who is completely fair and completely good."

Family Discussion
  1. Simeon and Levi's anger was understandable, but their response became evil. How do we pursue justice without becoming unjust in the process? What does "vengeance is mine, says the Lord" mean in practice?
  2. God sees Dinah even when the text mostly records the men's voices and actions. Who are the "Dinahs" in your world whose stories are not being heard? What does Jesus's pattern of stopping for the overlooked call you to do?
  3. This dark chapter is still in the Bible — God didn't remove it. What does it tell us about God that He preserves the honest record of human evil alongside His faithful covenant work?
Memory Verse
"Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.'"
Romans 12:19

Genesis 35 · Return to Bethel — Going Back to Where God First Met You

Genesis 35:1–15
God Calls Jacob Back to Bethel — The Place of First Encounter
▼
The Big Idea

After the disaster of Genesis 34, God told Jacob to go back to Bethel — the place where God had first appeared to him. This is the pattern of restoration: after failure, God calls us back to the place of first encounter. Jesus is always calling us back to where we first met Him.

📖 What the Verse Says

God said to Jacob: "Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau." Jacob called his household together: "Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments. Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone." They buried the foreign gods under the oak. They journeyed. God appeared again at Bethel and confirmed the covenant — "I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply." And Jacob set up a pillar and poured oil on it.

🔍 How This Points to Jesus

After the violence and deception of chapter 34, God does not abandon Jacob's family — He calls them back. Not forward to something new, but back to the place of first encounter. Bethel — "house of God" — was where Jacob first dreamed of the ladder to heaven, where God first confirmed the Abrahamic covenant to him personally. God calls Jacob back there to renew, confirm, and re-establish what had been compromised by sin and violence.

This is the pattern of Jesus's restoration throughout the Gospels. After Peter's three denials — the most catastrophic failure of his discipleship — Jesus met him by the Sea of Galilee and three times asked "Do you love me?" (John 21). He brought Peter back to the water — where it had all started. Back to the place of first call (Luke 5). Back to the beginning, to restore and recommission. Jesus always restores by bringing us back — not to condemnation but to the covenant, to the first love, to the altar that should have never been abandoned.

Revelation 2:4–5 — Jesus's letter to the church at Ephesus: "You have abandoned the love you had at first. Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first." The call is always the same: go back to Bethel. Put away the foreign gods. Change your garments. And build the altar again.

Before they went to Bethel, Jacob commanded: "put away the foreign gods." You cannot go to the house of God carrying the gods of this world. Before we can return to intimacy with Jesus, there must be a putting away — a repentance, a burial of the idols. Jacob buried them under an oak tree. They did not gradually fade away — they were deliberately buried. This is what true repentance looks like.

New Testament Connection

John 21:15–17 — Jesus restoring Peter at the place of first calling. Revelation 2:4–5 — "return to your first love." Luke 15:20 — the father running to the returning son — the Bethel restoration. 1 John 1:9 — confess, He is faithful to cleanse and restore.

For Little Ones

"After terrible things happened in Jacob's family, God said: 'Go back to Bethel — the place where I first met you.' Before they went, Jacob said: 'Everyone get rid of your false gods.' They buried all the idols under a tree. That's repentance — getting rid of whatever competes with God before returning to Him. Jesus said the same thing: 'You cannot serve two masters.' Whenever we wander, God invites us back to the place He first met us. He always knows the way back."

Family Discussion
  1. God called Jacob back to Bethel — the place of first encounter — after failure. Is there a "Bethel" in your spiritual life — a moment, a place, a time when God was very real to you — that you need to go back to?
  2. Jacob said "put away the foreign gods" before they went to Bethel. What are the "foreign gods" — the idols, the competing loves — that need to be buried before you can fully return to God?
  3. Jesus restored Peter not by ignoring his failure but by taking him back to the water and asking "do you love me?" Why does restoration require going back to the beginning rather than just moving forward?
Memory Verse
"Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first."
Revelation 2:5

Genesis 36 · Esau's Genealogy — The Line That Did Not Carry the Promise

Genesis 36:1–43
The Sons of Esau — What Happens to the Line That Rejects the Birthright
▼
The Big Idea

Genesis 36 gives Esau's entire genealogy — kings, chiefs, clans. Esau's line was large, powerful, and impressive by worldly standards. But none of it carried the promise of the Messiah. This chapter teaches that worldly greatness and God's chosen line are not the same thing.

📖 What the Verse Says

"These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom)." The chapter lists Esau's wives, sons, grandsons, chiefs, and eventually kings — "before any king reigned over the Israelites." Esau's descendants had kings before Israel did. Esau prospered. His line was impressive. He had moved to Seir (Edom) because "their possessions were too great for them to dwell together" — he and Jacob had too much between them. Esau's line filled the land and produced leaders, kings, and chiefs.

🔍 How This Points to Jesus

Genesis 36 exists to show us what the line that rejected the birthright looks like — and it looks successful by worldly standards. Esau had kings before Israel. Esau had more possessions than Jacob could share land with. Esau was, by every external measure, more impressive than his brother. And yet — the Messiah did not come through Esau. The promise was not in the impressive, the firstborn, the powerful, the wealthy. It was in the younger, the weaker, the one who had to flee for his life.

Hebrews 12:16–17 warns: "See to it that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears." The birthright — the covenant promise, the spiritual inheritance — was exchanged for immediate physical gratification. A meal. This is the warning of the entire chapter: do not trade the eternal for the temporary, the promise for the present, the Messiah for prosperity.

Romans 9:13 — "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." This is not emotional hatred — it is covenantal language: God chose Jacob's line, not Esau's, as the vessel of promise. Not because Jacob was better (he was a deceiver), but because God's election is sovereign and gracious, not meritocratic. The Messiah came through the line God chose — a line marked not by worldly success but by covenant faithfulness and divine promise.

And look what Esau traded his birthright for: a bowl of stew. Red stew — his nickname became "Edom" (red). He is defined forever by the moment he chose the immediate over the eternal. Jesus, by contrast, refused to turn stones to bread in the wilderness — He would not trade His mission for physical satisfaction. Where Esau sold everything for food, Jesus fasted forty days and held to the Father's word.

Jesus came through the despised line — not the impressive one (Matthew 1; 1 Corinthians 1:27–29). Genesis 36 shows Esau's line producing kings while Jacob's line produced slaves and shepherds. The Messiah came not from the line of kings-before-Israel but from the line that spent 400 years in Egyptian slavery. Paul says God "chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; God chose what is low and despised in the world... so that no human being might boast in the presence of God." The Esau chapter is the contrast that makes the Jacob line's eventual triumph unmistakably God's doing. Jesus, born in a stable in Bethlehem to a poor family from a ruined dynasty, is the final proof: God has never once chosen the impressive option.

New Testament Connection

Hebrews 12:16–17 — Esau as a warning against trading the birthright. Romans 9:13 — "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" — sovereign election. Matthew 4:3–4 — Jesus refusing to turn stones to bread, unlike Esau trading the birthright for food. 1 John 2:15–17 — do not love the world — the Esau warning applied to believers.

For Little Ones

"Esau had a lot going for him — he had kings in his family before Israel did! He looked really successful. But the Messiah — Jesus — didn't come from Esau's family. He came from Jacob's family. Why? Because Esau had traded the most important thing — God's promise — for a bowl of soup. He chose what he could see and taste right now over what God was promising for the future.
